#7692. After Weil Gotshal’s collapse, law firm merger interest heats up

Consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both said they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ collapse. (Photo from Shutterstock)

The fall of Weil, Gotshal & Manges is pushing law firm leaders to rethink strategy, and many are looking to find merger partners.

According to a Thursday story by Law.com, consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both said they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil Gotshal’s collapse.

“Many conversations were put on hold earlier this year to watch where the economy was going, how AI was going to effect the transformation of law firms,” Grossman told Law.com, adding that interest in mergers “was picking up over the summer, but now the pace is getting faster.”

“A large and growing group of firms want considerably larger balance sheets, greater long-term stability, more money to invest in talent and technology, and other advantages that come with scale,” Zimmermann added.

Lisa Smith of Fairfax Associates offered a slightly different read, telling Law.com that merger demand was already strong in 2026, and Weil Gotshal mainly added urgency for firms that were already considering deals.

“The lesson of Weil is that for firms that are looking to grow and looking to grow via merger or particularly for those starting to see some cracks in the firm, it’s important to go to the merger market while you’re still in a strong position,” Smith said to Law.com.

Smith suggested that firms should approach the merger market from a position of strength. Firms that wait until trouble sets in risk becoming what advisers call a “falling knife,” an unstable partner few want to take on.

“We’ve seen a number of occasions over the last few years where a firm needed to merge with a ‘white knight’ and can only get that when the firm is strong enough to be a desirable acquisition,” Smith said. “For firms that start to see signs that the future is going to be more challenging, it’s important to look at their options early.”

Amazon argues Perplexity's Comet tool is accessing the online shopping giant without authorization.

SAN FRANCISCO (CN) â âI really don’t know what to do with this case,â Senior U.S. District Judge Maxine Chesney said Friday as a legal fight between Amazon and Perplexity AI returned to her court.

By the end of the three-hour hearing, the Bill Clinton appointee had granted Perplexity’s request for a stay in discovery, saying it would keep costs down and give her time to consider a dismissal motion. Neither Amazon nor Perplexity immediately responded to requests for comment.

Perplexity is the developer of Comet, an AI web browser capable of shopping on Amazon, including by comparing prices and reviews.

Amazon argues the tool violates laws like the U.S. Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Chesney previously found that Amazon would likely succeed on those arguments â then a Ninth Circuit panel rejected her findings, sending the case back to her court.

In its ruling, the Ninth Circuit found Chesney erred in her analysis of rules prohibiting access âwithout authorizationâ or at a level âexceeding authorized access.â

“It is the user who âaccessesâ Amazonâs computers with the help of the assistant,” U.S. Circuit Judge Milan Smith Jr., a George W. Bush appointee, wrote for the panel. A claim by Amazon under the California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act failed under the same logic.

On Friday, Chesney asked Amazon and Perplexity how she should apply the panel’s ruling.

Hagan Scotten, an attorney with the firm Hueston Hennigan who is representing Amazon, told the judge there were new facts that the appeals court had not considered.

A new version of Comet had been released since the panel’s decision, Scotten said. He also said Perplexity employees had tested versions of Comet on Amazon.

Scotten also argued the panel did not fully understand how Comet works.

The judges, he said, mistakenly believed that Comet only shopped on Amazon when directed by a user to do so. In fact, he said, a user might simply ask Comet to buy an item, then the tool would go to Amazon without being “invited in.”

âPerplexity and Perplexity alone is sending the agent to Amazon, which answers the panelâs question about who is in control here,â Scotten said, describing Perplexity as a “rogue actor” that was violating Amazon restrictions on AI tools.

âYou are very persuasive,â Chesney told Scotten. Nonetheless, she said she was trying to be âvery careful [so] you donât take me down another path that results in a reversal.â

Representing Perplexity with the firm Quinn Emanuel, attorney Daniel Posner pushed back on Scotten’s claims, including the argument that facts had changed since the Ninth Circuit ruling.

Comet cannot access Amazon itself, he said. Instead, a user must give the AI assistant access to their Amazon account.

âThe user always directs the agent to do something," he said. “That is the underpinning of the Ninth Circuit ruling.”

Posner argued Amazon was “scraping the barrel” in an effort to save its case. He cited Amazon’s claims that Perplexity employees were accessing Amazon.

âAs I understand, the allegation is that some unspecified number of Perplexity employees used their own Amazon accounts to access Amazon," he said. “If that type of conduct is criminalized, that would hit the panel opinion head-on.”

#7687. Even justices have regrets

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In June 2023, the court decided Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. University of North Carolina, holding that race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina violated the Constitution. Chief Justice John Roberts’ majority opinion in the case, along with Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s concurrence, cited Justice Sandra Day O’Connor’s 2003 prediction in Grutter v. Bollinger that “25 years from now, the use of racial preferences will no longer be necessary to further” student body diversity.

But the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi: O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement. In interviews with her biographer after she left the court, O’Connor acknowledged that the 25-year figure “may have been a misjudgment.” When asked for a new estimate, she replied, “[t]here’s no timetable. You just don’t know.”

Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

#7685. Criminal law is constitutional law

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite. Whether you are a Supreme Court follower who usually shunts criminal law to the side, or an experienced criminal law reader who might enjoy some holiday dinner thoughts for your friends and family, this column seeks to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law – and perhaps show why that can be so interesting. To do so, I will scatter some examples from last term, drawn from my recently published Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Cases booklet. When explaining criminal law to your friends or just opining over Thanksgiving dinner, I’d like to show why your mantra should be “crim law is con law” and vice versa.

Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law

Every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship. Even non-lawyers know from film and TV that the prosecution’s high burden for proof in a criminal case is beyond a reasonable doubt. But do they know that this is constitutionally required? And perhaps more interesting, that this standard is nowhere, textually, in that document?

“[T]he Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged,” wrote Justice William Brennan Jr. for the Winship court. If only all Supreme Court decisions had such clear and succinct rule statements.

But why is this the rule? It is not found either in the body of the Constitution or in the Bill of Rights, which was adopted soon after the Constitution and focused largely on criminal law protections. Winship‘s answer: because that standard “dates back at least from our early years as a Nation,” “[i]t is now accepted in common law jurisdictions,” it is expressed “in many opinions of this Court,” and it has “long been assumed” to be “constitutionally required.” Thus history, tradition, and precedent support it. Perhaps most fundamentally, a high standard of proof, harder to satisfy than in civil law cases, is essential to fundamental fairness for the public as well as individuals charged with crimes. It is “indispensable to command the respect and confidence of the community” as well as “every individual” exposed to imprisonment. Or, as Justice John Harlan II wrote in an influential concurrence, this standard is “bottomed on a fundamental value determination of our society that it is far worse to convict an innocent man than to let a guilty man go free.”

There are almost no crimes mentioned in the Constitution

This sometimes surprises 1L students (and others). But the goal of the Constitution was to (re)describe a system of government, and form “a more perfect Union” after the prior Articles of Confederation had proved unsatisfactory. It was not to write a criminal code. The states were then (and still are) the primary forum for criminal law.

So the Constitution defines only one crime, treason (in Article III, section 3). It mentions a few others, like “Bribery” (in Article II, section 4) and “Breach of the Peace” with a general reference to “Felony” (in Article I, section 6). And of course the Impeachment Clause (Article II section 4) mentions “high Crimes and Misdemeanors,” without definition. Again, states were expected to take care of the substantive definition and application of virtually all criminal law. (However, as I explained some years ago, the First Congress in 1790 did enact over two dozen federal crimes.)

Yet a large focus of the Bill of Rights is criminal procedure

Three years after the Constitution was drafted, the Bill of Rights focused on criminal law rights in at least four proposed amendments (the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth). I won’t list the multitude of rights captured there, but they form the bulk of all criminal procedure law school classes today. The right to be free from unreasonable governmental searches and compelled self-incrimination, and the rights to counsel, jury trials, and no cruel and unusual punishments – and much more – are all embodied in the Bill of Rights.

One example from last term: in Villareal v. Texas, the court had to interpret the Sixth Amendment right to “Assistance of Counsel” to decide (unanimously) that a criminal trial judge can order that the defendant not discuss their ongoing testimony with their attorney during an overnight recess.

Why was the Bill of Rights so focused on criminal procedure rights? It’s a fun question to ask students, or at the Thanksgiving table if things get slow. Sooner or later someone gives the soundbite answer: “because most of the constitution’s framers were crooks.” They were certainly guilty of treason – then and still today a capital (that is, death penalty) offense, as well as other crimes (violence, destruction of property, incitement, and more). Had the revolutionary Framers been captured by the government (the British) they likely would have been hung. Instead, during the course of the revolution, numbers had been tried in absentia, found guilty by officials (not juries), and had their houses searched and occupied by troops. Cruel and unusual torture had been inflicted on some captured compatriots. When constitutional ratifying conventions demanded a bill of rights, protections from unfair criminal processes were therefore topmost on the minds of many drafters (if not perhaps “the People” at the time).

(Another aside: ask your lawyer friends to compare the content of civil procedure versus criminal procedure classes today. The latter full-semester course is almost entirely constitutional law – I used to call my own crim pro class “Con Law Three.” By contrast, civil procedure classes, also a full semester, focus largely on the nitty-gritty details of federal rules, only occasionally wandering into statutes or the Constitution.)

In addition to the four explicitly criminal-focused amendments, you might then add general constitutional ideas that are bound to capture some criminal law cases: the First, Second, Third, and Ninth Amendments. The First Amendment’s direction, that “Congress shall make no law” regarding (“respecting”) or abridging freedoms of religion, speech, and the press, is a constitutional law command against criminal laws as well as civil. So too is a protection of a right to keep and bear arms, and to not have government troops quartered in “any” house (not just your own).

And then consider the “great generalities” of the Constitution

In his 1921 Storrs Lectures at Yale Law School (subsequently published as “The Nature of the Judicial Process”), future Supreme Court Justice (and then New York Court of Appeals Judge) Benjamin Cardozo discussed “the great generalities of the Constitution.” Among these, the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the 14th Amendment are huge sources of criminal law doctrine. Just last term, for example, the procedural steps required to apply the Equal Protection Clause against racial (and other) bias in jury selection, and the idea that due process and judicial integrity requires a “miscarriage of justice” exception to guilty plea waivers, received focused Supreme Court attention (in Pitchford v. Cain and Hunter v. United States, respectively).

Criminal law cases focused on the meaning and application of these broad constitutional requirements arise regularly almost every Supreme Court term. Indeed, as I advise my students every year (again I aspire to teach with a smile, not didactic cynicism): no matter what arguments you make on the defense side of a criminal case, always add the words “and in violation of due process” to preserve at least a thread of a constitutional argument that you may not even perceive at the moment.

In addition to equal protection and due process, I (and others) would add the Ninth Amendment, which speaks of unspecified “rights … retained by the people.” Justices have sometimes suggested that the Ninth and Tenth Amendments state nothing but “truism[s],” while other Supreme Court decisions have relied (at least in part) on the Ninth. For some, invocation of the Ninth Amendment may provoke if not laughter (it having been referred to by one academic as a “constitutional jester”), then a distinctly conservative or “originalist” rejection. Yet other conservative scholars such as John Yoo and Calvin Massey (my late former colleague) have written expansively about it. As Randy Barnett has argued, the Ninth Amendment “means what it says,” and is “a significant guarantee of individual liberty.” If that is so, then it is (or could be) another source of criminal law protection for criminal defendants.

So criminal law is, very often, constitutional law

Thus it should be unsurprising (as detailed in my Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Law booklet) that 22 of the court’s merits decisions last term that address criminal law involved elements of constitutional law (17 fully argued cases plus five summary (unargued) decisions). That’s a substantial percentage of the court’s entire merits opinions docket, roughly a quarter or more.

Statutory criminal law cases also often involve constitutional law

By now I hope that you are persuaded: criminal law is (often) constitutional law. “But wait – there’s more!” When you combine the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause with the oft-cited judicial doctrine of constitutional avoidance, criminal cases requiring statutory interpretation also fall into this category. That is, these are criminal law cases that involve consideration of constitutional law. Advocates in statutory cases often raise potential constitutional objections to a criminal statute or to its application in their case, or they may raise constitutional law ideas in favor of their preferred interpretation. In addition, an understanding of constitutional doctrine can be necessary to properly evaluate the merits of a statutory claim. The bottom line is that, in many statutory criminal cases, explication or consideration of constitutional law is necessary or helpful to explain the result.

Just a few examples from last term: In Barrett v. United States, the court had to mine the details of double jeopardy doctrine to agree, unanimously, that a statute could be interpreted as not permitting two convictions for a single act, thereby avoiding a constitutional problem. In Olivier v. City of Brandon, the court had to examine Olivier’s constitutional claims in order to decide whether the federal civil rights statutes were a proper vehicle for him to sue under. And in Whitton v. Dixon, the court had to briefly explain the constitutional Giglio doctrine, regarding a prosecutor’s failure to disclose exculpatory impeachment information, to reverse an application of the federal habeas corpus statue.

Immigration cases also often require constitutional law, either to dispose of the merits or to resolve statutory issues in them. Last term’s birthright citizenship case, Trump v. Barbara, is the most obvious example. Because immigration and criminal law cases are often intertwined – consider recent ICE arrests, detentions, and criminal violation grounds for removal – I include them in my annual review as well as the purview of this column. And even civil cases that I consider related to criminal law often require consideration of constitutional law concepts. For example, last term’s Hencely v. Fluor Corp., rejecting a claim of government contractor immunity, required consideration of constitutional preemption doctrine.

In other words, criminal law mixed with constitutional law is everywhere.

Last week, many of us were focused on the details of elections around the country, big and small. And next week, after Thanksgiving, will be chock full of criminal law and related Supreme Court oral arguments. So I’ve tried to give you a break today, and provide a few thoughts that are, perhaps, entertaining, or provocative, or at least interesting ways to navigate your mealtime gatherings (rather than focusing on the usual subjects). For some of you, perhaps this column has simply demonstrated what you already considered obvious; or perhaps it has opened interesting linkages in your mind between constitutional law and criminal law. In any case, thanks for reading this far. Next week I hope you are fortunate enough to breathe relaxing breaths, give thanks, and dwell not on legal minutiae but on what really matters.

Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

Recommended Citation: Rory Little, Criminal law is constitutional law, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 20, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/criminal-law-is-constitutional-law/

#7681. Tubi wants more creator content. The Kickstarter-backed “Fandom Fund” is here to help.

As Tubi looks to bring more creators to its shores, it is helping them solve a prevalent problem by providing easier access to capital. That’s the gist of the $250,000 Tubi x Kickstarter Fandom Fund, which unites a Fox-owned streaming service and a 17-year-old crowdfunding platform.

The Fandom Fund follows up last year’s FilmStream Collective, a partnership between Tubi and Kickstarter that delivered support to more than 20 independent films. The new collab between the companies will function similarly; Tubi will throw its weight behind active Kickstarter campaigns, which it will distribute exclusively.

Tubi won’t just pick any Kickstarter project; instead, as it has done with its other incubator programs, it will hone in on the genres that have the widest appeal among its 110 million monthly active users. The categories fitting that description include horror, YA, Black entertainment, true crime, LGBTQ+, comedy, and reality.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Per Business Insider, $150,000 of the fund will be split between eight to 15 Kickstarter campaigns. The remaining $100,000 will go in one lump sum to a larger project.

For Kickstarter, the Fandom Fund represents an increasing commitment to the creator economy. It is part of the three-month-old Culture Fund, which builds on Kickstarter’s enduring status as a key tool for indie artists. In 2024 alone, the platform generated over $700 million of fundraising across more than 35,000 projects.

Indie creators don’t always get distribution deals with brand-name platforms, but Tubi is eager to support the next generation of storytellers — whom it believes are just as capable as traditional TV voices. To that end, Tubi has premiered a handful of shows and movies led by social media standouts. One of the projects in the Fandom Fund will get a similar treatment by receiving additional backing, allowing it to be developed into a full-length series or feature film.

“We believe great talent can come from anywhere,” said Tubi GM of Creator Programs and EVP of Business Development Rich Bloom in a statement. “The Fandom Fund gives emerging storytellers the resources to bring those ambitious ideas to life on a bigger canvas while preserving the creative voice, vision and ownership that made their work resonate.”

Kickstarter will provide updates about the Fandom Fund through its film-focused newsletter. Participation in the fund requires an active campaign, so if you want Tubi’s backing, get your crowdfunding game on.

#7674. Sick of pirates and freebooters? Meta brings its “content protection” tool to Instagram.

Pirated content has been an issue for Meta for so long that it was still known as Facebook when creators first fought back against so-called “freebooters.” To combat unauthorized reuploads, Meta brought a “content protection” tool to Facebook last year. Now, Instagram creators are getting access to that resource as well.

“Eligible creators” on Instagram can now enroll for access to the management system that was previously limited to Facebook. Like Facebook’s video rights manager, which was itself adapted from previous services like YouTube’s Content ID, the content protection tool uses fingerprinting technology to scan for uploads that are identical to an enrolled creator’s video.

Once a match is detected, Instagrammers can respond in one of four different ways: They can track the reupload (that’s the default option), request for it to be hidden, require the reuploader to add a credit link, or release their claim on the infringing video. Notably, creators cannot receive monetization through the reposts, as is possible through services like Content ID.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Meta has positioned itself as a champion of original, non-repetitive content. It updated Instagram’s algorithm, providing more visibility for creators who share their own work. Financial penalties for serial reuploaders came to Facebook in 2025, and further penalties arrived on Instagram this year.

Other platforms have followed Meta’s lead. YouTube cracked down on “mass-produced or repetitive” content in 2025. Earlier this year, Google’s video hub clarified that creators aren’t able to monetize “generic” uploads. Anything “unsatisfying or off-putting” — i.e. the sort of slop you’d expected a generative AI model to spit out — faced similar repercussions.

The link between unoriginal reuploads and AI slop is undeniable. Traditional studios have urged platforms to crack down on channels that use AI to steal from artists rather than executing original concepts. Those demands have led to new rules across TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram.

By bringing content protection to Instagram, Meta is setting itself up to take further action against AI slop in the future. An introductory post explains that “we’re also exploring different ways to limit the reach of content and profiles that use AI tools to post this type of content repeatedly,” so stay tuned for that if you’re sick of low-effort AI posts.

#7672. As Netflix and Disney sniff around, YouTube hypes its creators’ “world-class, studio-quality” programming at L.A. Premieres event

Tonight, YouTube brought back its film-festival-style event, Creator Premieres, to showcase a new batch of “world-class, studio-quality creator programming” coming exclusively to its platform.

Last year’s Creator Premieres–the first YouTube held–took place at New York City’s historic screening space Metrograph and showed off projects from creators like Ms. Rachel, Brave Wilderness, Dhar Mann, Deestroying, and Cleo Abram.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

This year’s edition was hosted by House Guest‘s Scott Evans at The Hollywood Roosevelt in L.A., and highlighted upcoming projects from YouTube OGs and greats like Emma Chamberlain, Nick DiGiovanni, Lilly Singh, Wesley Wang, Grace Reiter, and more.

Google President Sean Downey took the stage to highlight YouTube’s continued dominance on TV screens, and gave a nod to participating creators for fueling the UGC machine that keeps viewers coming back to YouTube–on TVs and across other devices.

Of course, he also appealed to advertisers in the same breath, reminding them that this “world-class” content is what they could be marketing alongside, if they cough up the cash to Google.

“YouTube creators are not just shaping modern culture, they are redefining the entire entertainment landscape. This slate of shows demonstrates how creators are commanding primetime attention on the big screen and building unmatched fan loyalty,” Downey said. “For brands, this isn’t about buying thirty seconds of ad space; it’s about moving past standard commercial breaks and partnering directly with the storytellers who are defining modern culture.”

YouTube has spent years at the top of TV watch time charts–a fact that really gets under the skin of competitor Netflix. Up till recently, though, Netflix’s main response to this irritant was talking a lot of sh*t about YouTube and occasionally signing back catalog deals with view-drivers like Ms. Rachel and CoComelon.

But in the last 12 months, something’s shifted. Netflix has begun tapping creators like Salish Matter, Alan Chikin Chow, and the Stokes Twins not for back catalog agreements, but for development deals–deals which result in exclusive original programming that won’t appear on YouTube.

And YouTube’s not happy about it. The platform has been offering creators money, including production financing and sweet ad deals, in exchange for turning down offers from Netflix. Conversely, creators who decide to sign with Netflix are put on YouTube’s naughty list, and denied perks like revenue shares from primo ad deals.

(That being said, Netflix-friendly creators aren’t entirely blacklisted. DiGiovanni signed a catalog crossposting deal with Netflix in July, and was still one of the headline creators at tonight’s showcase.)

The point we’re making here is this: With Netflix–and Disney–sniffing around, YouTube has more incentive than ever to hype up its creators and their projects on a big stage.

#7669. IShowSpeed hits the cover of LIFE Magazine on 90th anniversary of first issue

When LIFE Magazine relaunches on November 23, one of YouTube’s biggest streamers will be front and center.

IShowSpeed (aka Darren Watkins Jr.) has been revealed as one of five cover stars featured in LIFE ‘s relaunched debut issue, alongside fellow icons like Olympic skater Alysa Liu and actor John Malkovich.

The issue—which describes Speed as “arguably the most famous 21-year-old on Earth”—chronicles his streaming career thus far, before looking ahead to his upcoming goals (which include livestreaming from outer space and visiting every country).

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

“Nobody embodies our current moment like IShowSpeed,” Kieran Press-Reynolds, the LIFE writer who profiled Speed, said in his piece.

A feature in a legacy publication isn’t exactly groundbreaking for Speed, who has been included in multiple TIME magazine lists, teamed up with brands like Expedia, gotten his own Fortnite skin, and served as the poster child for the 2026 YouTube FIFA Creator Cup.

LIFE’s decision to feature Speed alongside an Olympic athlete and a Hollywood actor, however, is further evidence of traditional media’s growing acceptance of content creators as cultural heavyweights. Legacy publications have become increasingly eager to court creators—and woo their massive online audiences—in recent years. TIME unveiled its first-ever TIME100 Creators issue in 2025, while digital stars like MrBeast and Emma Chamberlain have served as the faces of Rolling Stone‘s own Creator Issue since 2022.

Just a few days ago, Hearst Magazines launched Hearst Creator Studios, a division that will bring original creator content to editorial brands like Cosmopolitan, Elle, and MotorTrend. Now, as LIFE returns 90 years after its first issue, creators are taking center stage at yet another legacy magazine dedicated to covering “the stories that define our time.”

#7668. GTA VI is smashing Twitch’s records—and it wants to make sure advertisers don’t miss out

Grand Theft Auto fans across the world are still eagerly anticipating Rockstar’s long-awaited sequel to roll out in their regions. But according to data from Streams Charts, GTA VI has already smashed multiple streaming platform records—including becoming “the most popular gaming category in Twitch history by peak viewers.”

As of publication time, GTA VI has attracted a peak of 3.29 million concurrent viewers on Twitch, 3.19M on YouTube, and 1.5M on Kick.Those totals put it “ahead of every previous game launch tracked by Streams Charts,” the data company said in its report.

Twitch isn’t taking all that buzz—or the dollar signs that come with it—for granted. But GTA also doesn’t exactly fit into the platform’s careful approach to brand safety. So, it’s introducing new tech to ensure that advertisers can cash in on the hype surrounding GTA VI without putting their brand reputations at risk.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Back in September, Twitch CEO Dan Clancy told hosts of The Snarketing Podcast that the platform had begun using AI to evaluate whether streamers are squeaky-clean enough for brands to run ads against their content.

“[W]e transcribe streams to figure out ‘Is this appropriate for this brand?’” he said. “So that’s something that we’ve had to invest a lot in to make sure that for a brand, their content is appearing next to creators and content that fits what they’re trying to do.”

That update didn’t come out of nowhere: Twitch has long asked streamers to label their content in certain circumstances where mature themes or imagery are involved.

As Gizmodo noted, this means creators have historically missed out on ad revenue when streaming mature-rated games, “because while streamers can receive donations from viewers, big-time monetization ultimately depends on advertising, and advertisers are generally skittish around things that might frighten the poor sensitive product-buying public.”

Last week, however, Clancy told Bloomberg‘s Romaine Bostick that “one of the challenges in this space is advertisers want to be part of the GTA 6 launch”—they just don’t want their ads to appear alongside the spicier parts of the game.

To solve that problem, Twitch’s new technology will allow brands to run ads on GTA VI streams while also ensuring that (as Clancy phrased it) “any of the parts of GTA 6 that they might not want to have their ads associated with, their ads won’t be associated with that.”

The ins and outs of how that system will actually work remain to be seen. But if it does prove effective for GTA VI, we’ll be watching to see whether Twitch expands the tech to other streams and genres previously dismissed as unsafe for brands.

#7663. Another Disney creator deal: YouTube illusionist Zach King joins the Mouse House

Disney continues to prove that Netflix isn’t the only competitor sniffing around YouTube‘s top talent.

For their deal, 36-year-old L.A.-based King will make 10 original short-form videos, which Disney will have exclusive rights to distribute. Disney says the agreement “will also bring [King’s] signature illusions to new content for Disney+ and [King’s] own channels inspired by Disney’s Hexed, Star Wars, and other Disney films and experiences.”

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

One of the King projects coming to Disney+ is Cardboard Wars, his 52-minute intentionally-low-budget tribute to Star Wars: A New Hope. King uploaded the film to YouTube in August, and soon will cross-post it to Disney’s streaming service.

But there’s still more: King will pop up on Disney’s social accounts as well, hosting behind-the-scenes content about the VFX and filmmaking techniques he uses in his content.

“I fell in love with filmmaking and storytelling as a young kid, grabbing my parents’ home video camera and teaching myself to edit,” King wrote in an Instagram post. “A lot of my early homemade films were inspired by the Disney movies and the behind-the-scenes footage they would show in the DVD featurettes. There was always a sense of magic I would see on the screen, and so I’m thrilled to be working with Disney to continue that magic of filmmaking for the next generation of storytellers.”

King has worked with Disney regularly in recent months: He was at its glitzy Created in L.A. event in September, and earlier this month played a game of viral format Cake or Fake? with Hexed (and Arcane, and Sinners, and Spider-Verse, and Hawkeye) star Hailee Steinfeld. But this is his first official, expansive content deal.

“Zach makes the impossible look real, bringing the kind of imagination and originality that has always defined Disney,” Asad Ayaz, The Walt Disney Company’s CMO and Brand Officer, said in a statement. “He brings both a filmmaker’s ingenuity and a fan’s passion to our stories, along with a unique connection with audiences. We want to build lasting relationships with creators like Zach, giving their ideas room to grow across Disney. That’s what makes this next chapter of our work together so full of possibility.”

As we mentioned above, everyone–including YouTube–has had their eye on Netflix’s obvious poaching efforts…leaving room for Disney to sneak in the back.

In the last couple months, Disney has announced deals with major creators Dhar Mann, Dude Perfect, and Like Nastya. Crucially, these are all development deals–the exact kind of agreement that has YouTube on guard with Netflix.

And Disney’s not quite showing its full hand just yet. During its earnings call Nov. 17, executives only mentioned YouTubers once, in passing and in reference to Disney+’s growing crop of approved creator content.

We suspect more is in the pipeline–and that YouTube may have to start paying creators to turn down Disney deals, too.

#7662. Canvas Worldwide’s Agentic Layer Helps Zillow Distinguish Real Renters From Dreamers

We’ve all been there: You look up a product out of sheer curiosity with no intent to actually spend money on it, and suddenly you’re inundated with ads for similar products.

The challenge for advertisers is distinguishing the passive browsers from the people with genuine purchase intent.

Zillow knows that challenge well. Its rental site often serves as a place for people to fantasize about their future home, even if they’re not actually looking to move.

“We are known for dreaming,” said Ravi Kandikonda, SVP of marketing for Zillow Group. But that’s not necessarily a bad thing. Welcoming the dreamers is a great way for Zillow to drive awareness of its brand and get potential future renters into its platform, Kandikonda added. From there, it’s a matter of striking a balance between building awareness and driving conversions.

That’s where Zillow turns to its media agency partner, Canvas Worldwide.

In September, Canvas announced a new division called ART Dept., which provides a collection of AI solutions to help brands and agencies optimize their campaign budgeting and pacing. Zillow is using ART Dept.’s AI agents to better separate the renters from the dreamers and tailor its marketing accordingly.

The “ART” in ART Dept. stands for “AI Applied Research and Technology.” (Though, if we’re being pedantic, wouldn’t that be AART – or AIART?)

Quibbles about acronyms aside, Canvas’ new division offers a mix of AI optimization features that are becoming commonplace for ad agencies and marketing platforms. Though, like other agentic platforms, Canvas says its differentiation comes from how it applies those optimizations to its agentic layer.

For example, offering a pacing dashboard is “table stakes” by now, rather than a distinguishing feature for an agency, said Sally Lee, SVP of programmatic and ART at Canvas.

But Canvas wanted to make its pacing dashboard “multidimensional” by connecting it with a budget source of truth and building an agentic layer on top of it, said Lee.

The agentic layer, called Talos, determines whether a campaign is underpacing or overpacing and optimizes for better performance. Before pushing the newly optimized campaign into the platform, a member of the Canvas team reviews and approves (or denies) it.

Canvas can “pick and choose from different search and behavioral categories” to optimize against, said Lee. In Zillow’s case, that might include whether a user is researching renter’s insurance or looking into moving truck rentals.

Canvas gets those behavioral signals through its data partnerships, including its MCP connection to predictive audience targeting company Dstillery.

Access to behavioral data has helped Zillow reach more specific audiences and be smarter about exactly where and when to target them, said Kandikonda.

For instance, targeting multifamily renters in Seattle using a generic, off-the-shelf “multifamily apartment buildings” audience only goes so far, he said. “I need to know when they are on a particular platform” to bid for that audience at the right moment with the right content, he added.

Dstillery’s audience modeling predicts which websites the target audience will visit and when based on real behavioral data. And Canvas’ AI can help surface audience and behavioral overlaps that might have previously gone overlooked by its team.

Canvas’ reliance on data-backed reasoning was a major draw for Zillow when the two first started working together in 2023, Kandikonda said, and it continues to be a major focus of ART Dept.

The goal behind the new product suite is to save media teams time figuring out what media is performing and how much to spend on different audience segments.

Increasing ROI is important for any brand. But it’s particularly important within the real estate market, Kandikonda said, as marketing dollars are constrained and the entire industry “is bouncing around the box.”

So, while Zillow appreciates its dreamer audience, it’s feeling the same pressure most brands are to focus on lower-funnel conversions, such as “actual movers,” Kandikonda said.

That’s part of the reason off-the-shelf renter audiences weren’t cutting it for Zillow’s ads business, he added.

An off-the-shelf audience may indicate people who are interested in renting more broadly, he said, but ART was able to select for people who were actively in the process of planning a move. And more precise targeting means better lower-funnel ad performance.

From Zillow’s perspective, the biggest change from using Canvas’ ART Dept. is the results, rather than the process. After all, the AI tools are used by the Canvas team, rather than by Zillow.

Zillow just tells Canvas what outcome it wants to achieve. Canvas then translates the desired outcome into a scorecard that weights different goals and metrics within the interoperable tech infrastructure that powers the ART Dept., which is called +Suite.

From there, Canvas’ Audience+ product (which is similar to a data management platform) connects to data partners and the Talos AI agent to build custom audiences. Finally, Talos activates and optimizes the campaign.

The system creates an ongoing feedback loop, said Canvas’ Lee: “Build an audience, activate it, see how it’s performing against what that client cares about and identify where to make changes to drive a better outcome.”

#7661. Only You Can Prevent JavaScript Security Hacks; AppLovin Eyes A Criteo Acquisition

Adding to the myriad IT outages and cybersecurity scares of the past month, a major malware attack recently hit 178 publications and organizations that use Optimizely’s A/B testing and analytics tools.

The list included the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, but the problem extends well beyond those high-profile sites. The issue is that many operators don’t audit the tech vendors that drop JavaScript onto their pages.

“We’re in the age of JavaScript supply-chain attacks, and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators,” Zach Edwards, a researcher for Infoblox and the co-founder of DecryptAds, tells Daniel Krebs of Krebs on Security.

The “content security policies” (or CSPs) Edwards refers to set limits on what third-party code can do on a site, including what it can load or inject. Of the 178 affected Optimizely accounts, only 24 had CSPs in place and enforced them. Those 24 didn’t spread the malware.

Because the malware ran in the site’s JavaScript, visitors to pages without CSPs could be infected simply by loading the page – no click or scroll required.

The main offender, btw, in terms of third-party JavaScript abusers that expose sites to hackers, is ad tech, of course. It’s not even close. Which is why, unfortunately, as Krebs notes, downloading a modern ad blocker is the best solution for consumers to protect themselves.

The rumor mill is heating up as the year winds down.

Criteo has been part of that chatter for a while, with private equity firms Vista Equity and Quinti Capital reportedly interested in taking it private. Criteo hasn’t exactly thrived as a public company, after all.

But it does possess an immense graph of shopper info.

And now another contender has reportedly entered the ring. According to Reuters, AppLovin is among those in talks with Criteo.

Big companies can use deal talks to get an inside look at the finances and operations of smaller companies. Even if the deal doesn’t happen, they’ve still gotten a peek under the hood.

Amazon, for example, was rumored to have considered Criteo once upon a time – not long before launching its own off-site retargeting. Hmm.

But Criteo would be an interesting fit for AppLovin. It plugs into a wide network of retailers and web publishers – an entirely new arena to AppLovin, which operates almost entirely in-app – and would bring a large book of business with ecommerce companies. AppLovin has said that it’s a priority to add advertisers to its “consumer” segment, which is primarily ecommerce.

Criteo would offer a cheat code to get there.

The rise of residential proxy services that hide bot traffic behind real human IP addresses has been a boon for ad fraud. Often, consumers aren’t even aware they’re acting as a proxy for bot traffic.

Now, cheap consumer electronics with backdoor vulnerabilities built in can deliver billions of fraudulent ad impressions per day, according to a new report by HUMAN Security’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research Team.

The latest scheme Satori uncovered, which it dubbed BADBOX 3.0, was responsible for 40 billion fraudulent bid requests a day at its peak. It used the same residential proxy infrastructure as two other fraud rings that were uncovered by Satori in the past two years – hence the “3.0” branding.

The infrastructure relies on cheap TV sets manufactured in China by a company called TXCZ. These TVs have backdoors in their operating systems that allow fraudsters to compromise them.

Once they’re compromised, the TVs run video ads in the background that the TV owner cannot see. The bid requests for these ads use the TV owner’s IP address to appear as if they’re targeted to a real human. They also impersonate traffic from legitimate CTV apps.

People who bought one of these TVs pretty much had no chance.

“It was compromised before you plugged it in: playing video ads you could never see and quietly renting out your home internet connection to strangers,” says HUMAN’s Gavin Reid. “Neither the advertisers paying for those ads nor the people who bought the boxes had any idea.”

YouTube adjusts its video view counts with modeled co-viewers based on its estimate of how many people saw the screen. [The Verge]

#7656. Measuring Clicks Is Making ChatGPT Ads Look Like A Bad Bet

The first question marketers ask about every new advertising channel is almost always the same: Does it perform better than the last one we tested?

It happened with social. It happened with retail media. And now it’s happening with OpenAI.

The debate around ChatGPT advertising has quickly become a comparison with Google Search. Can it deliver lower CPAs? Does it convert as well? Is it ready to compete for performance budgets?

They’re all understandable questions. But they’re the wrong ones.

It’s a mistake to assume conversational AI should behave like search in the first place. The customer journey is fundamentally different. If marketers continue evaluating ChatGPT using search-era metrics, there’s a real risk they’ll dismiss one of the most significant new advertising channels before they’ve understood how it creates value.

Google built the world’s most successful advertising business by harvesting intent.

If a user searches for “cheap hotels in Hawaii,” Google shares a list of relevant results. The commercial intent is already there. The advertiser’s job is simply to be the most relevant answer when the purchase decision is made. But conversational AI works differently.

Instead of typing in a few keywords, a user might go into detail and explain that they’re travelling to Hawaii for a friend’s wedding, that they’re on a tight budget but want their own room, oh, and they’d like to surf while they’re there. That’s no longer a search query; it’s a conversation. And that difference matters.

Rather than simply capturing existing demand, conversational AI helps users explore options and refine priorities before they buy. When the traveler eventually visits the website to book, they’ve often already used AI to compare all the alternatives and understand exactly what they’re looking for.

The advertising opportunity is participating in how intent develops.

One of the first things marketers notice when they begin testing conversational AI is that the acquisition metrics can look uncomfortable.

CPAs can appear higher than those achieved through search. For anyone used to judging performance through traditional attribution, that’s an easy reason to conclude the channel isn’t competitive.

If it looks like search and behaves like search, surely it should produce similar economics. But once you step back and look at the customer journey rather than the click, that conclusion becomes much harder to support.

A user spending several minutes discussing products, asking follow-up questions and refining their requirements is behaving very differently from someone typing a short keyword into Google. They’re effectively qualifying themselves before they ever reach an advertiser’s website.

That means acquisition might cost more, but the customer arriving at the other end can also be significantly better informed and a much stronger commercial fit.

Judging conversational AI purely on CPA risks confusing efficiency with effectiveness.

The measurement frameworks we’ve inherited aren’t suited for where the consumer journey is going.

For more than two decades, performance marketing has been built around clicks because clicks were observable. Attribution models rewarded whichever interaction happened closest to the conversion, giving marketers a practical way to optimize campaigns at scale.

That made perfect sense in an internet dominated by search engines, display advertising and relatively linear customer journeys.

Conversational AI changes that, because the interaction influencing a purchase often happens long before a click ever occurs. And when the eventual conversion happens later through another channel, traditional attribution naturally gives the credit elsewhere.

That doesn’t necessarily mean the initial conversation had little value; it simply means the measurement framework wasn’t designed to capture it.

Early evidence suggests that when marketers move beyond attribution and begin measuring incremental business outcomes instead, conversational AI looks very different from the picture painted by last-click metrics.

AI advertising can work very effectively. But unless marketers are measuring it in a way that reflects how the channel actually influences buying decisions, it can create a colossal education gap.

The conversation today largely centers on whether OpenAI can compete with Google.

A far better question is whether conversational AI should be evaluated like search at all.

Every evolution in advertising has forced marketers to rethink measurement. Social wasn’t simply another display channel. Retail media wasn’t just paid search inside a retailer’s website. CTV couldn’t be judged solely through linear TV metrics.

Conversational AI deserves the same mindset shift.

Google monetized search intent. Conversational AI has the potential to monetize the conversation that creates it.

Those are fundamentally different commercial models. If marketers continue measuring one using the rules of the other, they risk underestimating not only the performance of OpenAI ads, but the role conversational AI is likely to play in the future of digital advertising.

#7654. Meet OpenX’s New CEO, An Optimistic Realist

Safari is cracking down on identity vendors, DSPs are going direct to publishers, Google gets to keep AdX, agents are threatening to cut out the middlemen, the walled gardens keep winning and the open web is under pressure.

In early November, OpenX named Robert Horler as its new CEO, taking the reins from interim chief Joshua Metzger, who returned to his role as chief legal officer.

Horler joins at a time of upheaval for the ad industry and one of readjustment for OpenX. In January, the company lost John “JG” Gentry, its CEO for nearly 15 years, after a long battle with cancer.

A 30-year veteran of agencies, advertising and ad tech, Horler previously ran Dentsu Aegis Network in the US and Northern Europe, was COO of Quantcast and, most recently, led creator agency Whalar as chief exec before it was acquired by Accenture earlier this year. He’s still on the Whalar board.

But, given the state of the industry, how was Horler feeling roughly a week in at OpenX? Not too bad. He’s a glass-half-full kinda guy, but he’s also a pragmatist.

“Everybody’s being disrupted,” Horler said. “You can pull the blanket over your head and say, ‘No thanks,’ or you can see an amazing amount of opportunity for companies that are agile and ambitious. I fancy our chances.”

Horler spoke with AdExchanger about Apple’s latest move, whether the sell side has the upper hand right now and the big boots he has to fill.

AdExchanger: Let’s start with the state of play. The assumption for a long time was that as the line blurred between the buy side and sell side, DSPs would come out on top. Now it feels like the sell side has the power. Is that how you see it?

ROBERT HORLER: I’d agree, but it’s complicated. The pendulum has swung toward supply because advertisers want to get closer to the data and the publisher.

For the first time in about 30 years, the bigger agencies are pursuing divergent strategies for how they work with SSPs and DSPs. They all want more control, more orchestration and more influence over the revenue they drive, and I’d hypothesize that SSPs are well placed to deliver that.

Also, no slight to The Trade Desk, but if the biggest cat in the jungle is having this many existential challenges, that tells you something’s going on.

Speaking of big cats, OpenX is suing Google, as is Magnite, PubMatic and Index Exchange. I know there’s not much you can say about OpenX’s lawsuit, if anything, but as an industry observer, what did you think of the fact that Google didn’t have to divest AdX in the federal ad tech antitrust case?

You know, it’s a shame. It’s tough for everybody who thought there would be one, but I can’t say that I’m surprised there wasn’t.

A lot of sell-side players are going buyer-direct. So is everything just everything now? Are the distinctions between buy-side and the sell-side tech no longer meaningful?

For the people who aren’t in it, who don’t work in ad tech or programmatic advertising – and that includes some clients – the lines have always felt quite blurred. That’s not new.

There’s probably not as much difference now as there was, though. Things are converging and overlapping and people are encroaching a bit into each other’s territories as they figure out the brave new agentic landscape. And, of course, there are also pressures that exist within their own businesses.

But what will always be true is that publishers want to generate as much yield as possible and advertisers want to pay as little as possible, as long as it’s still effective, of course. So, yes, perhaps those lines are blurring a bit, but this natural tension will always exist.

I know you’re still settling in, but how about you approaching Apple’s move to block identity vendors in iOS 27?

That’s all I can say right now other than that no one here is walking around and behaving like it’s an extinction event or something.

You spent the better part of a decade on the buy side, including as the US CEO of Dentsu. What do buyers get wrong about the sell side?

I’d flip it, actually. The sell side needs to be simpler to partner with and more able to adapt, and sometimes they forget that. The sell side also underestimates how overwhelmed buyers are with choices.

If you show up with an overly complex sell or a raft of products that you can’t explain in simple language, you’ll just sound like everyone else. Also, don’t underestimate the importance of humanity. Trust is built around people, not just technology.

I wanted to ask about John. He was such a lovely man, and his death was such a loss. How will you keep his legacy alive?

I never got to meet him, and I really wish I had. He was clearly beloved. When I came in for my board interview, I read the remembrance book here and it was really moving. It made me think, “If I get this job, those are big boots to fill.”

The best way to honor him is to continue the mission and build a valuable company where people enjoy coming into work. John clearly believed culture is preeminent and that it’s the people who make a great company, and I want to lead with that in mind.

This interview has been lightly edited and condensed.

#7653. Netflix is rallying post-Warner Bros. with revised IRL installation plans and a potential bid for NBCUniversal

OK, so Netflix failed to buy Warner Bros. Discovery.

That potential acquisition is apparently top of wishlist for Netflix (and Variety already deemed it “Hollywood’s Next Big Deal”), but Comcast co-CEOs Mike Cavanagh and Brian Roberts say they’re not selling.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Well, according to Bloomberg, the current plan is for Netflix to revamp its approach to permanent interactive IRL installations, aka Netflix Houses. The streamer first unveiled these in 2023, with a demo setup that looked like someone stocked the gift shop in Jurassic Park with merch of the laser murder doll from Squid Game.

At the time, Josh Simon, Netflix’s then-VP of Consumer Products (now CEO of collectibles company Funko) said the concept for Netflix Houses came from knowing “fans love to immerse themselves in the world of our movies and TV shows,” and “thinking a lot about how we take that to the next level.”

Netflix had flirted with pop-ups before that; those were mainly focused on selling stuff. Make no mistake, Netflix Houses are also focused on selling stuff, but in a Disney World kind of way, where fans pay $39 to enter the House and head through an art gallery-esque space filled with themed exhibits like exclusive theater shows, movie/TV set recreations, VR experiences, and arcade games. There are cafeterias and merch shops, but by and large the things to buy share billing with things to do.

The Houses are permanent installations (for now just in Dallas and Philly, with one planned to open in Vegas in 2027) but the exhibits within rotate regularly to keep up with whatever’s trending on Netflix.

This year, for example, the Houses were renovated to feature animated smash megahit KPop Demon Hunters. They’ve also spotlighted Stranger Things, One Piece, Wednesday, and the aforementioned Squid Game.

Per Bloomberg, Netflix initially planned to open dozens of Houses across the U.S., focusing on quieter suburban areas away from downtowns. It wanted to snap up spaces in malls, which are not doing very well and might be willing to rent for cheap.

But apparently the results from its first two Houses haven’t been quite what Neflix expected, so it’s pausing openings beyond Vegas until it can reassess.

People familiar with the matter told Bloomberg the Philadelphia location has daytime draws like mini golf and a movie theater, but doesn’t see much traffic at night. Dallas, meanwhile, is breaking even financially, and has done well with larger groups and corporate events.

Netflix is also planning to see what comes from its Las Vegas location. Vegas, as you may know, is not in fact a quieter suburban locale–so if the House there proves to be profitable, with more traffic than Dallas and Philly, Netflix could reconsider where it opens in the future.

People familiar with the matter said Netflix is also looking at maybe taking Houses overseas. But wherever the next one ends up, it probably won’t open for at least another year, they said, until significant data from all three flagship U.S. locations is in.

Now, with all this in mind, it’s worth remembering Netflix just shock-fired its longtime Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria and replaced her with Peter Rice, Disney‘s former General Entertainment Chairman. Film chief Dan Lin is out too. Clearly, Netflix hopes to revamp more than its IRL installations…and perhaps it’s hoping Rice’s Disney EXP comes in handy with the Houses?

#7651. Growth Copywriter at Winona

Winona is one of the leading telemedicine companies providing HRT for women in menopause. We’ve built all of our technology in house including an EHR, patient care admin system, patient portal, website, marketing technology etc. Winona has two compounding pharmacies and a team of in house physicians providing world-class care via a fully vertically integrated business model.

We are looking for a data-backed, empathetic Growth Copywriter to own the performance and optimization of our end-to-end messaging ecosystem. At Winona, copy isn’t just about sounding nice. It’s a measurable variable in our growth funnel. You will design and execute rapid copy experiments across our paid acquisition, intake flows, and lifecycle retention loops to help women confidently access bioidentical HRT and menopause care.

Full-Funnel Experimentation. Write copy hypotheses, design rapid A/B tests alongside growth and analytics teams, analyze performance data, and turn winning variations into a scalable messaging playbook.

Lifecycle Growth & Retention. Write, test, and optimize automated onboarding, activation, adherence, churn-save, and win-back sequences across email, SMS, and push notifications to drive LTV.

High-Intent Conversion Surfaces. Own the persuasive strategy and microcopy for landing pages, interactive quiz/intake flows, checkouts, and dynamic pricing/offer messaging.

Paid Acquisition at Scale. Generate volume-driven concepts, hooks, and static/video copy variants for Meta, Google, and YouTube, systematically iterating based on creative testing data.

Voice of Customer (VoC) Intelligence. Continuously mine product reviews, customer support tickets, intake data, and exit surveys to isolate deep qualitative insights and high-converting customer language.

AI-Augmented Workflows. Leverage and train Winona’s internal AI copywriting tools to scale production velocity, maintain brand consistency, and build automated variant pipelines without sacrificing quality.

5+ years of dedicated copywriting experience specializing in direct-response, conversion copywriting, or growth marketing.

DTC Telehealth, Wellness, or HealthTech experience is highly preferred. You understand how to write about sensitive health topics with clinical authority and deep empathy.

A portfolio backed by data and results — the exact copy variants you tested, the structural or psychological changes you made, and the quantifiable lift they produced in metrics like CTR, quiz completion, or conversion rates.

Deep lifecycle marketing mastery: significant experience building and optimizing automated email and SMS flows (onboarding, retention, win-backs), rather than just writing one-off promotional campaigns. You know how to nurture a lead over time.

A strong foundation in A/B testing mechanics — comfortable formulating clear copy hypotheses, understanding sample size requirements, and knowing when a test result has achieved true statistical significance.

The balance of empathy and compliance: a proven ability to write about highly sensitive personal health topics (menopause symptoms, hormonal changes, wellness) with profound empathy while strictly adhering to healthcare compliance rules and ad-network medical restrictions.

An experimenter’s ego — you don’t take copy critiques personally. You’re obsessed with letting consumer behavior and performance data crown the winning angle.

As a full-time member of our team, you’ll enjoy:

Paid non-working holidays per country of residence

Medical/ Dental/ Vision insurance (US-W2)

Employee engagement activities and virtual gatherings

#7650. Don’t Give Privacy Regulators An Excuse To Come Knocking

And so it makes sense for contracts to always meet the strictest combination of state requirements.

But it’s a massive chore, and everyone – colleagues, partners, ad vendors – want to know why a contract that’s worked for years suddenly needs a rewrite, Turner said. They pummel him with questions.

“Sometimes I’ll just turn off the microphone and scream into the wall briefly,” Turner joked, “because nobody hears you when you scream in space.”

The latest addition to Turner’s ever-growing to-do list comes courtesy of Delaware.

In programmatic advertising, though, vetting every partner in the supply chain would be a massive headache. A single ad campaign can bounce data between dozens of middlemen, measurement vendors and tracking pixels.

And if every company in the chain sends every partner its own custom questionnaire, said Michael Hahn, the IAB’s SVP and general counsel, “we drown ourselves in paperwork, and nobody is any safer.”

“It requires a contract at each hop,” Eakins said, “because each hop is a transaction involving personal data.”

In other words, the days of box-ticking and boilerplate are finally over.

Paperwork isn’t compliance, said Courtney Cantor, deputy general counsel at PubMatic, who regularly fields a steady stream of due diligence requests.

“It’s no longer about just putting the right contracts in place,” Cantor said, “but actually having evidence to show if a regulator came knocking on your door.”

Although that’s assuming contracts reflect reality, which often isn’t the case.

Take the standard clause requiring a vendor to delete everything when a customer agreement is terminated, said Gary Kibel, a partner at Davis+Gilbert. Not only do most companies not remember to do that; it’s often impossible.

“I can’t delete everything” is the correct response to any deletion request, Kibel said, because vendors have legal and record-keeping obligations of their own. On top of that, if businesses purge all of their data, they can’t do business. If you delete a client’s email address, for example, then how do you chase an unpaid bill?

The fact is, managing retention – which Turner referred to as “the ‘R’ word” – is borderline impossible, he said.

“Everybody puts it in their agreements; everybody says how long they’ll keep things,” Turner said. “But I guarantee that if I went to every single person in this room’s company and looked at your data, I’d find retention violations everywhere.”

It’s not malicious or anything; it’s just incredibly difficult to do. “I don’t mean to inspire any attorneys general,” Turner said, “but I think it’s an area we all have to be really careful about going forward.”

Although there’s a heck of a lot of low-hanging fruit to go after first. You’ve gotta get the basics sorted or you could be screwed.

“I had a client about a year ago that got a letter from the Delaware attorney general’s office and they raised that issue,” he said.

“The simple, easy things,” Turner said, “don’t let them be a problem.”

And also don’t forget that regulators are also just people, he said – people who read the news. When one company gets sued or fined, other states take notice and start wondering whether the same thing is happening in their backyard.

Not that getting a letter from a regulator is necessarily a DEFCON 1 situation.

These types of inquiries can feel scary because they often contain detailed questions, Kibel said. Regulators do their homework before reaching out. But a letter isn’t a formal legal demand, and companies don’t technically have to respond.

It’s always a good idea to engage, though, Kibel said.

Ignoring outreach from a regulator is a surefire way to turn a voluntary back-and-forth into a subpoena.

Kibel has put clients on the phone with regulators in the past, and the vibe was usually as pleasant as could be expected. “It wasn’t treated like a deposition,” he said, “and it wasn’t a hostile setting.”

Because regulators do “understand that every system is not 100% perfect,” Kibel said.

“But they also do want to see that you’ve thought about these issues in advance,” he said, “and that you’re being forthright with them in terms of answering their questions.”

Ideally, the whole thing gets worked out over a few phone calls and never escalates.

Likewise, the purpose of Delaware’s HB 380 isn’t for the AG’s office to chase down and investigate every single third party, Eakins said. The hope is that companies and their counsel do the policing themselves.

“The goal is for the industry, for you all, to be saying, ‘You know what, this counterparty is just too much of a high risk,’” Eakins said. “I don’t trust what they’re doing with the data, so we’re just not going to take that reputational risk.”

#7646. TikTok’s CSAM Problem; You Can’t Bank On Data Security

Different advertisers have different brand safety thresholds, but there are some topics that no one wants to be associated with. First and foremost: child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

That risk is now playing out in Spain, where several advertisers paused their TikTok ads this week.

Last week, Spanish news outlets reported that multiple advertisers – including Banco Santander and energy company Moeve – had suspended their TikTok campaigns after ads from major Spanish brands had appeared alongside CSAM on the platform.

Videos that either included CSAM or featured websites that sell CSAM ran before or after ads from 21 brands, Digiday reports, including Banco Santander, Samsung, Ralph Lauren and Pringles.

TikTok has avoided taking direct responsibility in its recent statements, assuring advertisers and agencies in a note that it is “deeply committed” to ensuring that TikTok is a safe platform for teens and that it has a task force addressing the issue.

“We condemn child sexual abuse and exploitation,” a spokesperson tells Digiday (uh, duh), adding that it’s “categorically prohibited” on the platform.

But, so far, these statements have done little to convince advertisers to return.

“Until we know what’s happening, it’s better to pause,” Laura Camazón, head of digital and innovation at Mediaplus Equmedia tells Digiday. So far, three of the agency’s clients have paused their TikTok activity.

In a week of mass technology service outages across America, Chase wants you to know that its regular service has not been disrupted.

However, one or more of Chase’s third-party tech vendors was the victim of a cyberattack. “We believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” the bank wrote in a statement on Thursday.

Mastercard and Visa were also tagged by a ransomware hacker org that leaked customer data. Credit card numbers were not compromised, but the data included some customer details. A Mastercard spokesperson described the leak as only touching a “limited amount of information from a subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program,” The Wall Street Journal reports.

The disclosures leave many key questions unanswered. None of the companies has named the vendors involved or specified whose data was exposed and what it included. For example, did the leaked data belong to cardholders who consented to having their data used for marketing and analytics? That would be an interesting wrinkle.

Chase was a little more specific about next steps, though, at least.

“Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring,” it said in its response.

On Thursday, Anthropic IPO’d at a cool $2 trillion, making it the first of the leading AI companies to go public.

Its share price opened at $111.50, then dropped to roughly $100 within its first hour on the market.

The timing is striking. Anthropic’s public launch comes just a week after ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down from his role at the company, following a leaked affair with a woman rumored to be a Chinese spy.

Huang’s departure left a gaping hole in AI funding. The industry may miss him for other reasons, too, but the bigger concern is capital.

“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Shamillah Bankiya, a partner at Dawn Capital, tells TechCrunch. Colette Kress, Huang’s temporary replacement as Nvidia’s CEO, is expected to be “much more conservative,” another investor adds.

Still, Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO goes to show that the AI bubble isn’t at risk of popping quite yet.

But it certainly “contrasts with an anxious moment for investors,” The New York Times writes, amid growing concerns over AI regulation and public backlash against the technology.

#7642. Q3 In Review: Pay TV Shrinks, Streaming And Sports Step Up

Have you been keeping up with the quarterly earnings scoreboard for media and entertainment companies?

It’s a lot, we know. Not to worry. We figured you’d be busy, and so we tuned in to Q3 call after Q3 call so you didn’t have to. (You’re welcome.)

Before you hunker down for Turkey Day, here’s a rundown on the TV and streaming companies (those that remain after all the recent consolidation, that is) that posted their earnings for the three months ending on Sept. 30 – and what these reports reveal about the state of TV and media today.

Netflix’s Q3 numbers look decent on paper. Revenue rose 12% year over year to $12.9 billion, while advertising revenue alone has spiked over 80% this year. But Netflix wasn’t able to double its ad revenue again this year as planned. To be fair, growing ad revenue quickly was easier to do back when Netflix first started its ads biz from scratch.

On the advertising front, Netflix also touted improved programmatic targeting and ad measurement capabilities, including a pixel to measure conversions.

Comcast’s media division reported $5.4 billion in earnings last quarter, a 13% YOY jump from this time last year. Alongside NBCUniversal, which Comcast plans to spin off as a standalone company alongside British broadcaster Sky, Comcast’s media division also includes NBCU’s Peacock, Telemundo, Bravo and Universal film and television studios.

But Comcast had weaker performance across the broadband and theme park sides of the business, which saw a 6.1% revenue decline. (The theme parks live under the Universal brand and will go with NBCU and Sky in the spin-off.)

Unlike Netflix, Fox boasted of recent boosts in engagement. Its free ad-supported TV platform, Tubi, saw a 23% YOY increase in viewing hours, thanks in part to the platform’s recent focus on creator content.

Zooming out from Tubi, Fox’s overall revenue rose 22% to $4.6 billion last quarter, including a 47% jump in advertising revenue. But, sports and streaming aside, it wasn’t all sunshine and rainbows. Fox News saw major viewership declines throughout the year and into October, when total-day ratings fell 27% ahead of the midterms.

Fox was vague about details regarding its acquisition of Roku but asserted it expects to close the deal soon. A mere few days later, on Nov. 6, Fox announced it officially completed the acquisition.

Versant Media, which spun off from Comcast in January, posted a 4% decline in Q3 revenue, a loss it mostly blamed on secular declines in the pay-TV industry.

Versant also closed its acquisition of Full Swing last quarter, a deal that supports its ambitions to lean on live sports – golf in particular – as a competitive advantage.

Skydance closed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 4, so there were no WBD-specific numbers in its Q3 report. But WBD aside, Skydance reported $7 billion in revenue last quarter, representing 5% YOY growth.

Streaming was a highlight, with Paramount+ revenue jumping 21% YOY to just over $2.1 billion. Skydance also announced plans to launch a service combining HBO Max and Paramount+ at the beginning of next year.

Skydance CEO David Ellison confirmed that Paramount+ and Pluto are officially operating on the same ad tech stack, noting that integrating HBO Max should be a relatively speedy process.

Disney reported a 16% revenue jump to $25.9 billion in Q4 (its fiscal year ends in September) and a revenue increase of 8% to $102.3 billion for the full year.

Ad revenue grew 10% to $1.7 billion within Disney’s entertainment segment. For its sports segment, that growth rate was 20%.

Disney also shared that it’s unifying Disney+ and Hulu into one app beginning next month. The company will add more sports to Disney+ in December and introduce creator content from TikTok into the Disney+ mobile app.

Sports streamer Fubo, which also ends its fiscal year in September, saw its fourth-quarter revenue inch up to $1.5 billion from $1.48 billion during the same period last year.

But Fubo suffered a net loss of $51.8 million in its Q4 – a heavier loss than the $38.8 million it posted in the same quarter last year. Fubo attributed the loss to operational and restructuring costs related to its recent merger with Hulu + Live TV.

Philips Sonicare, a maker of electric toothbrushes and water flossers, decided to consolidate its streaming TV ad buys within Amazon, which has also been doing some consolidating itself.

#7641. TikTok’s next microdrama is an 81-episode musical series from Barlow & Bear

Four and a half years after winning a Grammy for The Unofficial Bridgerton Musical, the songwriting duo known as Barlow & Bear has something new in store for TikTok viewers.

Abigail Barlow and Emily Bear are two of the creators behind To Die For Love, an 81-episode musical microdrama co-produced by TikTok and Ampersand. According to TikTok, the series follows “an ambitious half-witch vying for her coven’s crown. When she falls for a mortal, their romance takes an unexpected turn, forcing an impossible choice between family and the love of her life.”

Barlow & Bear created an original score for To Die For Love, while Barlow co-wrote the script alongside Oscar-nominated writer/director, actor, and opera singer Julia Aks.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Barlow also stars in the series opposite Broadway vet Derek Klena. Executive producers include Ampersand CEO Agnes Chu, Benj Pasek, Justin Paul, Danielle Perelman, Chris Crema, Matthew Ko, and Kevin Weaver.

“Making To Die For Love has been one of the most rewarding creative experiences of our careers,” Barlow and Bear said. “We love a pressure cooker, and building an entire musical in under five months proved that meaningful storytelling isn’t about time—it’s about the story and the people bringing it to life.”

This isn’t the first creator-driven microdrama TikTok has brought to life. Earlier this year, Issa Rae’s media company, HOORAE, struck a deal with the platform to produce short-form web series for both TikTok and its companion app PineDrama. The first vertical series to emerge from that partnership, Screen Time, had racked up over 620 million views on TikTok and PineDrama as of late October, making it both platforms’ most-viewed show to date.

TikTok doubled down on that success last month when it announced a new microseries-focused partnership with Made By Us Studios, which describes itself as a “first-of-its-kind, Hollywood-grade studio designed for the creator economy and powered by creator management company MADE BY ALL.”

Now, TikTok is forging ahead into the world of musical microdramas. To Die For Love will be available exclusively on TikTok and PineDrama, with all 81 episodes premiering December 21. The original soundtrack will be released by Atlantic Records.

#7639. Have a Merry Ads-mas

We use Outlook at AdExchanger, and last Wednesday everything came crashing down. PR people resorted to frantic texts to reach journalists. No emails showed up in my inbox for 18 hours. But ad tech soldiered on. We open the episode with a check-in about last week’s historic outage and some of the surprising takeaways for ad tech from this flurry of outages.

Then, what do we know about the state of the growing app economy? Plus, compared to TV, ad units on mobile apps go for a fraction of the price.
