#7532. Federal funding for public media is coming back, one way or another. But is it time for a deeper rethink?

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Congressional Democrats will have to determine whether they want to revive the old system Donald Trump defunded or build something more attuned to today’s media ecosystem.

It was 318 days ago that the Corporation for Public Broadcasting — the primary funder of public media in the United States since 1967 — officially ceased to be, the victim of Republican budget cuts and years of attacks from Donald Trump. CPB is not “on pause” or “in hibernation” — it’s dead. As its final CEO Patricia Harrison put it: “CPB’s final act would be to protect the integrity of the public media system and democratic values by dissolving, rather than allowing the organization to remain defunded and vulnerable to additional attacks.”

You may have heard, however, that we had some elections in the U.S. recently, and the Republicans who defunded NPR and PBS will no longer control the House of Representatives or Senate as of January 3. In their place will be Congressional Democrats much more favorable to public media. So it seems quite likely that the federal government’s next budget will re-fund it rather than de-fund it.

But with CPB officially no more, Democrats will have a rare opportunity to rethink the system from scratch instead of just prescribing minor tweaks to funding levels. The media environment of 2027 will, it goes without saying, be radically different from 1967’s. Over-the-air broadcasting is no longer America’s dominant medium. The immensely profitable newspapers that were the bedrock of news back then are shells of their former selves. And what was once a highly localized information ecosystem has been thoroughly nationalized and globalized, with access to news increasingly determined by a few large tech platforms. Democrats could just revive the old LBJ-era model — but should they instead build something new?

These questions will dominate the next year of discourse around public media, and interested parties are already laying out plans. This morning, the Roosevelt Institute released a new white paper titled “Creating a New U.S. Public Media System: Normative Arguments and Policy Options.” Written by Penn professor (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Victor Pickard, it argues for a thorough reinvention:

Taken together, the 2025 federal defunding of American public media, the ongoing collapse of local journalism, growing media oligarchy, a multitude of social harms arising from unregulated platforms and AI technologies, and other political and economic challenges to our media and democracy demonstrate the need for robust public media systems. Fundamental flaws — especially its funding mechanisms — are baked into the historical U.S. public media model, and they must be structurally addressed. The current crisis presents a unique opportunity to create an entirely new kind of public media system based on a local “Public Media Center” model. Pickard lays out three core ideas: de-privatization, democratization, and localization. De-privatization means more thoroughly removing “public” media from the interests of the private sector. No more sponsorship messages from Monsanto or ExxonMobil, no more need to pitch corporations or beg listeners for the funds needed to pay reporters. Pickard wants the public media system to be entirely publicly funded, to the tune of roughly $30 billion a year. That would be a massive increase — almost 60×! — from the pre-Trump level of federal funding, which was around $500 million a year. Even if you include all non-federal sources of revenue, $30 billion would still represent a public media system 8 to 10 times larger than what exists today. (Pickard dreams big!) RELATED ARTICLEDo countries with better-funded public media also have healthier democracies? Of course they doJoshua BentonJanuary 24, 2022But the fact that $30 billion sounds enormous is mostly about how small U.S. public media has always been compared to its international peers. Before defunding, the U.S. spent roughly $3 per person per year on public media. Compare that to countries like Norway ($110), Finland ($101), Denmark ($93), the U.K. ($81), France ($76), Czechia ($60), Japan ($53), Australia ($36), and Canada ($27). If Pickard got his $30 billion wish, U.S. public media funding would sit at about $88 per capita — BBC territory, roughly speaking. But even getting to the level of Canada or Australia would represent a huge increase. By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades: Endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence. Toward this aim, a public media system should not be public in name only but actually owned and controlled by local communities. To encourage trust and community investment, this collective ownership and governance must translate to public participation in all stages of media production and dissemination. In fact, public media institutions are often cross-ideological islands of trust in an otherwise dismal landscape. This trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

Pickard lays out three core ideas: de-privatization, democratization, and localization.

De-privatization means more thoroughly removing “public” media from the interests of the private sector. No more sponsorship messages from Monsanto or ExxonMobil, no more need to pitch corporations or beg listeners for the funds needed to pay reporters.

Pickard wants the public media system to be entirely publicly funded, to the tune of roughly $30 billion a year. That would be a massive increase — almost 60×! — from the pre-Trump level of federal funding, which was around $500 million a year. Even if you include all non-federal sources of revenue, $30 billion would still represent a public media system 8 to 10 times larger than what exists today. (Pickard dreams big!)

RELATED ARTICLEDo countries with better-funded public media also have healthier democracies? Of course they doJoshua BentonJanuary 24, 2022But the fact that $30 billion sounds enormous is mostly about how small U.S. public media has always been compared to its international peers. Before defunding, the U.S. spent roughly $3 per person per year on public media. Compare that to countries like Norway ($110), Finland ($101), Denmark ($93), the U.K. ($81), France ($76), Czechia ($60), Japan ($53), Australia ($36), and Canada ($27). If Pickard got his $30 billion wish, U.S. public media funding would sit at about $88 per capita — BBC territory, roughly speaking. But even getting to the level of Canada or Australia would represent a huge increase.

By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades:

Endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence. Toward this aim, a public media system should not be public in name only but actually owned and controlled by local communities. To encourage trust and community investment, this collective ownership and governance must translate to public participation in all stages of media production and dissemination. In fact, public media institutions are often cross-ideological islands of trust in an otherwise dismal landscape.

This trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

And for Pickard, localization is a logical response to the de-localization of media that the internet hath wrought. Many public radio and TV stations primarily serve as distributors of national content, in large part because funding is nowhere near robust enough to create enough local programming to fill each day. And no matter how much you like Ken Burns or All Things Considered, sending the same programming nationwide can limit the range of a community’s residents who might be interested. He advocates pushing more control away from a federal-level entity like CPB and toward states, counties, and cities via block grants.

Pickard describes the nodes of this system as Public Media Centers: “multimedia hubs that are federally guaranteed but locally owned and democratically governed,” which “would provide journalism, broadcasting, digital media, and other information services based on community needs.”11“Public Media Centers” is also what Pickard called them in one of his first public articulations of the idea, in his 2021 prediction here at Nieman Lab. Some might be housed in existing public radio or TV stations, others in post offices or libraries. And individual communities would be able to determine which media formats work best for them, rather than being locked into the expensive broadcast infrastructure required to reach audiences in 1967.

I am obliged to note that there are a huge number of barriers to Pickard’s vision becoming reality. Most obviously: $30 billion a year is a lot of money. That’s around the annual budget of the federal school lunch program ($32 billion), FEMA ($32 billion), or NASA ($25 billion). Secondly, the commercial media industry would not sit quietly while the federal government funds an enormous new rival that doesn’t need to sell ads or subscriptions. (For context, the entire U.S. newspaper industry pulls in around $20 billion a year in revenue.) And American suspicion of “state-funded media” goes deep enough that I can’t imagine Democrats looking to retake the White House in 2028 deciding this is the hill to die on.

But the new Congress is still weeks away from convening, and the next federal fiscal year starts more than 10 months from now. This is the season for big dreams, for expanding the edges of the Overton window, and in that sense, Pickard’s ideas should give newly empowered policymakers a lot to think about.

#7530. A Charity Rescue Dog Outscored Amazon’s Christmas Ad – PPC Accounts Need A Story Before Cyber Week via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Give holiday Google Ads a stronger story: DAIVID ranks Dogs Trust above Amazon among 75 Christmas ads, guiding four creative changes before Cyber Week.

If you run paid media in the United States, the most useful creative test of the 2026 holiday season has already been run for you, on the other side of the Atlantic. A ranking of 75 U.K. Christmas ads by DAIVID, released Nov. 16, 2026, says a 60-second charity film about a boy and a scruffy rescue terrier is out-emoting Amazon, John Lewis, and M&S.

You have about two weeks before Cyber Monday and roughly five before Christmas to decide whether your Performance Max and Demand Gen asset groups carry anything that makes people feel something, or just a product carousel and a discount.

The rest of this column explains why a UK ad chart matters to a Google Ads account in Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, or Montana, where I think the data needs ground truthing, and what to change in your accounts this week.

Start with the money. According to Alphabet’s Q3 2026 earnings release, YouTube ads brought in $11.21 billion of the $82.01 billion in Google advertising revenue for the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2026. That works out to about 13.7%, the same share YouTube held for full-year 2025 ($40.37 billion of $294.69 billion). Across the last four quarters, the share has stayed between 12.8% and 13.8%.

Search is still Google’s biggest ad business, at $63.35 billion, up 12%. But two remarks from the Oct. 28 earnings call show why creative quality is now a search marketer’s problem, too.

Google’s CFO Anat Ashkenazi said YouTube advertising revenue rose 9%, “with Brand driving the largest contribution.” Brand advertising is exactly what UK Christmas ads are.

Google’s Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said Google has “integrated our AI creative tools directly into AI Max” and that Gemini models “helped advertisers generate over 1.5 billion campaign assets, up over 7x year-over-year.”

Google is making creative abundant – when anyone can generate a thousand headlines, images, and video cuts at no extra cost, sheer volume of assets stops being an advantage. What stays scarce is an asset that actually moves people, and that is what DAIVID’s chart tries to measure.

See also: Why Brand Advertising Matters For Paid Media Performance

The conventional wisdom says Brits start Christmas advertising right after Halloween while Americans wait until after Thanksgiving. This year’s data say American advertisers have moved earlier.

In a Tatari survey of 41 U.S. TV advertisers, 37% planned to go live in early November and 17% as early as October. Only about one in four planned to wait until Thanksgiving week. Yahoo DSP’s 2026 Holiday Shopping Study, as reported by Chain Store Age, found that 77% of advertisers planned to launch holiday campaigns by November.

The UK treats Christmas ads as a public event. Hero films drop in early November, the trade press reviews them within days, and testing firms publish scores while the season is still running. U.S. brands rarely publish anything comparable before Black Friday.

And most U.S. accounts will head into the peak with old creative. Tatari found only one in five of its advertisers producing net-new Black Friday Cyber Monday spots. A scored set of 75 fresh holiday ads is the closest thing to a free creative pretest you will get this year.

Amazon’s 2026 film, “Joy Delivered,” is a global campaign that also runs in the U.S., and it placed second in DAIVID’s UK chart.

See also: How To Evaluate Creative Performance in Meta Ads (and What To Test)

Dogs Trust’s “Kira Needs A Happy Place,” made by Girl&Bear Studios, the production arm of VCCP Blue, is predicted to trigger intense positive emotions in 58.4% of viewers. DAIVID says that is 20% higher than the average ad. Compared with the average, the film generated more than twice the levels of empathy (+120%), hope (+111%), gratitude (+110%), trust (+106%), and adoration (+102%).

Amazon’s “Joy Delivered” came second at 55.2%, and Not On The High Street’s “The Birdhouse” came third at 54.0%.

Lidl UK, Christian Dior, John Lewis, Arsenal FC, M&S, Disney, Barbour, and Shelter fill out the top 10. Gap, TK Maxx, Aldi, and Boots just missed.

DAIVID CEO and founder Ian Forrester said, “Dogs Trust has beaten some of the biggest names in advertising by getting one of the fundamentals right: making people feel something. Its story of a boy and his rescue dog generates particularly strong levels of empathy, hope, and adoration, showing that audiences don’t necessarily need spectacle, celebrity, or big-budget production to connect with a Christmas ad.”

Forrester added, “Amazon and Not On The High Street also perform strongly, while the presence of brands such as Lidl, John Lewis, and M&S in the top ten shows there are different ways to make an emotional connection with audiences.”

Dogs Trust is a charity, and the star of its film is a real rescue dog.

See also: How To Run Profitable YouTube Ad Campaign Without 7-Figure Budgets

I apply the same test to an ad-testing vendor that I apply to Google’s own performance claims. What exactly is being measured, and how big are the differences?

Start with the fact that these are predictions. DAIVID’s methodology says its AI models, trained on tens of millions of human responses to ads, forecast how viewers would feel.

Nobody sat a fresh panel in front of “Kira.” That makes the chart fast and cheap, which is the point. It also means DAIVID’s claim of performance improvements above 20% is the vendor’s claim, not an independent finding.

The spread is narrow, too. Dogs Trust leads Amazon by 3.2 points. Below the top three places, four through joint 10th sit within 0.9 points of one another, from 53.7% down to 52.8%. I would not tell a client that Lidl beat John Lewis on the strength of 0.3 points.

Last year’s DAIVID, Disney’s “Best Christmas Ever,” scored 58.2%. This year’s winner scored 58.4%. Even the best Christmas storytelling in Britain leaves about four in ten viewers short of intense positive emotion.

My view is that this chart is most useful as a creative brief rather than a leaderboard. The winners share a pattern you can copy into an asset group tomorrow. A simple story. A character the viewer roots for. Very little product on screen until late. And the emotions a discount banner can’t produce, especially hope, gratitude, and trust.

Here is what I would do with the time left before Cyber Week.

Audit Your Asset Groups For A Story: Open your Performance Max asset groups and Demand Gen campaigns and look at the video assets. If you haven’t uploaded a video, Performance Max can build one from your images and text, and it will look like it. Add at least one advertiser-made video, even a 15- or 30-second cut, which tells a small human story before it shows a product. Then review what Gemini generated for you. With 1.5 billion assets coming off the line, the default output drifts toward the same product-on-white look your competitors are getting.

Test Story Against Offer, With A Real Control: Set up a Demand Gen A/B experiment that splits traffic between an emotional cut and your standard offer-led creative. Keep audiences, bidding, and budgets identical so creative is the only variable. Ten days won’t settle it, so plan to run the test through the December shipping deadlines and read conversion volume alongside cost per conversion.

Watch Branded Search As The Bridge Metric: Brand ads earn their keep in a search account by creating demand you harvest later. Before the story asset goes live, record your branded query volume, branded impression share, and branded conversions, then check them weekly through December. If you meet the spend thresholds, a Brand Lift study with search lift will give you Google’s read on whether the video drove searches for your brand. Treat that as Google’s measurement, and compare it with what your branded Search campaigns actually show.

Rerun What Has Already Worked: Amazon reran its 2023 film “Joy Ride” as its 2025 holiday hero ad after it tested strongly, and shifted the production savings into media, according to DesignRush. If you have a past holiday video that performed, put it back into Demand Gen and Performance Max rather than replacing it with a weaker new cut made to hit a deadline.

I have covered paid search since 2003, and for most of that time the industry optimized the parts of an ad a machine could measure, like bids, keywords, and landing pages. Google’s AI now automates those parts and fills accounts with generated creative. That leaves one input a PPC manager still controls, which is whether the creative makes anyone care.

A rescue terrier outscored Amazon this year. Your holiday budget deserves at least one asset that tries.

#7529. Instagram adds Stories editing

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform rolled out various updates for the format, including the much-requested option to make changes to Stories after posting.

Instagram has rolled out a range of updates for Stories, including a much-requested editing option, which will enable users to update their posts after publishing.

As shown in this image, Instagram users will now be able to edit published Stories for up to 15 minutes after posting. Which isn't a huge window of time, but it should be enough to catch and correct any typos or mistakes.

It’s a significant update, which will be particularly beneficial for social media managers, enabling them to revise their content instead of having to start over again.

Instagram has also made it easier to select and post multiple images in Stories and added more display options.

It's also launched an updated sticker selector with new stickers, as well as expanded color gradient options for photo backgrounds in Story frames.

The updates will provide more ways for users to share their experiences in Stories during the upcoming holiday season, while as noted, they'll also help marketers use Stories to promote their holiday offers.

On another front, Instagram added the capacity to search saved items in the iOS version of the app.

As shown in these images, posted by app researcher Radu Oncescu, Instagram users can now search within their saved items. It’s a minor functional addition, but it could be a big help in finding previously saved posts.

#7528. Election season lifted public radio sites. So did a Supreme Court scandal and license plate drama.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

Stations in New Hampshire, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and Utah all climbed in our regular ranking of public radio stations between July and September.

More than a year ago, NHPR reporter Todd Bookman started asking questions about “an irregular personnel maneuver” involving the chief justice of New Hampshire’s Supreme Court. Bookman’s reporting ultimately became “Exhibit A” in the ethics probe that led to the justice’s resignation in September.

The bombshell resignation news was NHPR’s biggest story in September — and of 2026 to date. The story helped push NHPR up several spots in our regular ranking of public radio websites. NHPR saw visits rise 22% that month, according to Similarweb visit figures compiled by Nieman Lab.

RELATED ARTICLECollaborations and primary elections boosted traffic to public media sites this quarterNeel DhaneshaJuly 29, 2026At the very top of the list, not much moved. The Chicago Sun-Times, owned by Chicago Public Media, held onto the top spot, followed by Gothamist (from WNYC) and Minnesota Public Radio. As Nieman Lab senior writer Joshua Benton wrote when introducing the rankings, which we’ve also done for local newspapers and local nonprofit news sites, not all markets are created equal. Public radio stations serving major metropolitan areas with lots of college graduates have a bigger potential audience than stations serving smaller communities and areas with fewer resources. And, of course, Similarweb provides an estimate; internal metrics may differ. Still, the rankings are a valuable window into some industry-wide trends, and often an opportunity to highlight local news organizations punching above their weight.

Like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. New Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, said NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier. “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said. “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added. On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.” BREAKING: Fearless reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026 WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September. Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped. “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.” “Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also important to take advantage when it delivers,” she added. Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said. Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.” The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15. According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary. “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.” And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.” “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.” If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers. “The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.” Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah. Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total users are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill. All in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case. “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%. Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit. “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.” Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story. Like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. New Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, said NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier.

“But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said.

“[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added.

On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.”

WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September.

Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped.

“We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.”

“Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also important to take advantage when it delivers,” she added.

Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said.

Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.”

The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15.

According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary.

“We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.”

And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.”

“I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.”

If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers.

“The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.”

Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah.

Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total users are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill.

All in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case.

“Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%.

Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit.

“We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.”

Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.

#7527. Google Told CMOs To Stop ‘Top 10’ Listicles. Here’s Its Example via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Give your brand more opportunities to appear in AI-generated answers. Learn how YouTube SEO can support your visibility.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Finalize your AI search priorities for 2027 with the SEJ Newsroom and industry experts. Free • Live online • December 9, 2026.

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Google's marketing account told CMOs that their content is why they're invisible in Search. Here's what the article behind the post asks brands to do.

Google told CMOs through its Think with Google account on Nov. 19 that “AI didn’t make your brand invisible in Search. Your content did.”

The post pairs “Stop the ‘Top 10’ listicle” with “start leading with first-hand expertise.” That first half drew questions from SEOs on X about whether Google is telling brands to drop listicles. The October article the post links to is more specific. Its example is a generic “Top 10 Things to Consider” post, the same kind of post Google Search’s own AI guide cites as commodity content.

The article appeared Oct. 14 on Think with Google, the company’s digital marketing publication. Written by Brendon Kraham, Google’s VP, Search & Commerce Global Ads Solutions, it encourages brands to create specific content that draws on their own expertise and to measure their plans by leads or sales.

Kraham structures the article around three top priorities that he has heard from CMOs, which cover the “super-empowered consumer,” establishing the brand as an authority in its area of expertise, and creating measurable business results.

Think with Google summarized its advice to CMOs in this three-point cheat sheet.

The “Top 10” reference is found in his section on developing expertise, where he writes:

Take a running store, for example. Instead of publishing a generic “Top 10 Things to Consider,” they could create a deep-dive video analyzing exactly why a specific customer’s running shoes collapsed. That isn’t a generic review anyone could have written. It’s highly specific, real-world advice.

On measurement, he tells CMOs to keep planning “based on real business goals like leads or sales, not unproven proxy metrics.”

Lily Ray, who founded Algorythmic and specializes in SEO and AI search strategy, referenced the post on X and exclaimed, “Wow did Google really just tell CMOs to stop with the top 10 listicles?”

Ray is no stranger to tracking self-promotional “best” listicles, where a company lists itself as #1. In a June column for Search Engine Journal, she also reported that many of Google’s AI Overview results cited such listicles along with recommendations for other companies.

Growth advisor Eli Schwartz posted his version of the three steps “without being sanitized by the PR team.” Next to “Stop trusting proxy scores,” his post reads, “AEO VISIBILITY IS NOT REAL.”

Ross Hudgens, founder and CEO of Siege Media, replied to Ray, “Not of the type you’re thinking of. :)”

Google Search’s guide to optimizing for generative AI features, published in May, draws the same line as Kraham’s article. It gives “7 Tips for First-Time Homebuyers” as an example of commodity content, which it says is “often based on common knowledge.” The guide contrasts it with a first-hand piece about waiving a home inspection.

Neither the article nor the guide mentions self-promotional “best” lists.

When this content from Google reaches a CMO, the article it links to provides the recommendations in detail; it also has the same criteria for evaluating planned tips posts as does Google Search’s guide. Go through each of these individually, first asking if each represents something you have learned firsthand or simply restates common knowledge.

For self-promotional “best” lists, look to Ray’s tracking data instead.

Google shares major updates to its Search documentation on the documentation updates page, which also offers an RSS feed. Following the feed is an easy way to keep up with changes as they’re posted.

Featured Image: Remo_Designer/Shutterstock

#7525. LinkedIn study explores B2B buying decisions

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The research highlights the importance of relational factors, such as testimonials and peer validation, when it comes to influencing client purchases.

LinkedIn has published new research which examines what drives B2B buying decisions, and provides guidance on how brands can ensure that their products are as appealing as possible to prospective clients.

The study, conducted in conjunction with WARC and Lions Advisory, analyzes the factors that go into creating "buyability." The authors examined 700 B2B case studies in order to discover the crucial factors that influence purchase decisions across these examples.

The findings show that many of the key factors that drive decision-making are relational, as opposed to being grounded in product functionality.

As explained by Mimi Turner, global head of thought leadership strategy at LinkedIn’s B2B Institute: “Confidence in product capability is still very important. But once baseline requirements are met, the top priority is no longer marginal product superiority or price. It becomes whether the decision can be successfully defended even if outcomes go wrong.”

In order to test this, the study measured each of the 700 campaigns against various criteria related to buying signals.

The researchers then segmented the campaigns into "high buyability" campaigns, which were those that included three or more of these signals, and "low buyability" initiatives, which included zero, one or two signals.

The results shoed that high buyability campaigns — meaning those with more focus on testimonials, peer validation and measures of industry leadership — significantly outperformed low buyability campaigns across commercial and brand measures.

“Evaluated against the WARC B2B Effectiveness Ladder, High Buyability campaigns were also 1.7x more likely to be classified as ‘Strategic Assets,’ the highest rung of effectiveness, reserved for initiatives that drive sustained commercial growth,” Turner said.

The data also found that customer-centric insights were present in 83% of high buyability campaigns, which were also four times more likely to feature customer testimonials.

In other words, including more elements that reinforce buying decisions through relatable examples and external validation can have a major impact on reassuring buyers and securing more deals.

LinkedIn further tested these concepts in a campaign for ServiceNow, which specifically focused on these buyability elements.

“The results included a 10x increase in consideration, a 13x increase in unaided brand awareness over three years, and subscription revenue up by 23% over the same period,” Turner said.

Turner said these findings indicate that recommendations, relationships and relatable buying situations can have a significant influence on campaign outcomes.

These notes could help B2B marketers improve the resonance of their campaigns.

From YouTube views to crypto hacks, subscription cyclones to Czech hats: Have you kept up with this week’s media news?

It’s been yet another busy week. Recap it with the fourth edition of the Nieman Lab News-About-News Quiz, your weekly incentive to keep up with the latest happenings in the world of digital journalism. All questions are based on the week’s Nieman Lab stories or articles elsewhere that we’ve linked to in What We’re Reading. This is the final edition of the quiz for 2026; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027. Good luck!

The Chicago Sun-Times announced a new slogan this week. What is it?

“Chicago’s Paper” replaces “The Hardest-Working Paper in America,” the paper’s slogan since 2018.

An “overwhelming majority” of American journalists employed by this company voted this week to authorize a strike.

“The union has been negotiating a new contract for more than a year, and leaders say disagreements over wages, artificial intelligence and manager overreach have forced them to take this step.”

A “digital experience platform” company whose software runs on many news sites was hacked this week, sending malware to readers of the BBC, CNN, and Fox News. What’s the company’s name?

The hack stole cryptocurrency and credit card numbers from an unknown number of news site visitors.

A major journalism school announced this week that its master’s degree programs would now be tuition-free for in-state residents. Which school?

“Newmark J-School’s campaign for free tuition is rooted in CUNY’s decades-long commitment to access and opportunity for New Yorkers. At a time of profound transformation in the news industry, removing the cost of tuition makes it easier for more people to take the risk of entering the field.”

At this week’s summit in China, Bloomberg TV reporter Annmarie Hordern asked Donald Trump whether he felt Nvidia founder Jensen Huang had been disloyal to the United States. What happened next?

“It was the latest example of China’s strict controls on news coverage and how tightly Beijing tries to stage-manage major international events.”

Paid digital subscriptions at McClatchy-owned publications — a group that includes the Miami Herald, the Kansas City Star, and the Charlotte Observer — have declined how much in the past year, according to an internal corporate presentation?

Unique visitors have also dropped by 39%. McClatchy’s response? Doubling down on AI.

This is the per capita annual funding for public media across a set of five rich countries: $110, $81, $53, $27, $3. Name the five countries, in order.

With prospects for public media brighter with a Democratic Congress, some advocates are calling for a big increase in the United States’ historically puny funding levels.

YouTube has found a new way to inflate the number of “views” a video on its platform gets. What is it?

“YouTube, which has become even more popular on TVs than phones, also says the change will help it align with ‘TV industry standards,’ which similarly record views by estimating the number of people watching shows.”

In Czechia, mass rallies in support of public broadcasting have featured protestors wearing a very specific hat. Whose hat is it?

Since 1965, Večerníček (a diminutive of večerník, meaning evening newspaper) has appeared on Czech Television every night at 6:45 p.m. to wish children goodnight. Demonstrators wore his hat during the country’s largest protests since 1989 to oppose government plans to scrap public media license fees.

#7522. Why Building Trust Through Real People Stands The Test Of Time In SEO & AI Search via @sejournal, @lilyraynyc

Give your brand more opportunities to appear in AI-generated answers. Learn how YouTube SEO can support your visibility.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Finalize your AI search priorities for 2027 with the SEJ Newsroom and industry experts. Free • Live online • December 9, 2026.

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

For 20+ years, Google has warned against scaled, automated content, and AI slop is just its latest form. I believe focusing marketing efforts on real people with lived experience is the best antidote.

When it comes to organic search marketing, a loophole is not a strategy. Loopholes have expiration dates, and in many cases, the time spent chasing them would have been better spent on work that doesn’t backfire later on.

Any SEO who has worked in the field for a while has inevitably lived through a seemingly endless loop of fads, hype cycles, and shortcuts aimed at tricking search engines (and now, AI systems). Exact-match domains, article directories, parasite SEO, guest posting at scale, PBNs, programmatic pages, and now the AI-generated listicles, scaled AI content, and “inauthentic mentions” of the GEO era. Most of these things work for a while… until they don’t. And once Google, Bing, and more recently the AI companies themselves crack down, the sites that leaned on these approaches often end up worse off than if they’d never tried them at all, sometimes spending years cleaning up while traffic, visibility, and leads stay suppressed.

Plenty of people in this industry have battle scars from these experiences, myself included. My first real SEO wins came from buying links in 2010-2011, and Penguin erased them in a single morning in 2012. Six years later, the 2018 “Medic” update hit a client of ours that had been using AI and automation to scale medical content (long before this was popular), and it was the hardest hit from an algorithm update that I had experienced firsthand since the Penguin update. I think these scars are the badge of honor that inevitably comes with experience in SEO: thinking you know better than Google, and learning the hard way that you almost always don’t.

All of that said, there is one investment that has held up through every one of those cycles, and it’s the same approach I’ve recommended for many years: investing in real humans and placing them at the center of your marketing strategy. As AI makes generic content nearly free to produce, I believe that real, identifiable experts are becoming the clearest antidote to scaled, machine-generated slop. This article covers why, what the evidence shows so far, and how brands can consider “human-centric marketing” as a bigger part of their strategies.

The list of spam violations Google laid out back then has carried on, in some form, for more than 20 years, right into the AI search era. I put together this infographic showing how Google’s original spam policies map to popular GEO tactics we see today with AI search:

Automation in particular has been in the crosshairs for well over a decade. In August 2010, Google’s John Mueller told a site owner that publishing Google Translate output directly “could be seen as creating auto-generated content, which would be against our Webmaster Guidelines,” and recommended having a human correct it first. By 2012, Google had published a dedicated help page on automatically generated content. Its examples included text “translated by an automated tool without human review or curation,” Markov chains, automated synonymizing, scraped feeds, and “stitching or combining content from different web pages without adding sufficient value.”

For what it’s worth, I still see this exact issue affecting sites today – perhaps more than ever – including companies who come to me after experimenting with scaled AI translations that get little human review. It’s interesting that John’s 15+ year old answer still holds up, although to be fair, most site owners have never read Google’s guidelines (and nobody can be expected to know about a forum reply from 2010). That’s what their SEO experts are (supposedly) there to help them with.

Funny enough, that 2012 list reads a lot like the sales pitch for the same AI content tools that have recently captured the attention of C-level marketers everywhere, many of which work in ways that come very close to (if not directly violate) Google’s long-standing anti-spam policies. It’s not a huge surprise that so many of the sites featured in their case studies have since rapidly lost organic traffic.

Google’s wording has evolved since then, but the thread running through it has stayed remarkably consistent. In February 2023, a few months after ChatGPT launched, Google said it has “many years of experience dealing with automation being used in an attempt to game search results.” Then in March 2024, Google launched the scaled content abuse spam policy, which applies whether content is made “through automation, human efforts, or some combination of human and automated processes.” Automated translation, synonymizing, and stitching are still on the list, 14 years later. Marketers are now using LLMs to experiment heavily with all three. The main difference now is that generative AI sits at the top of the list of examples.

Across more than 20 years of guidelines, the common thread is fairly simple: content made for search engines at scale, with no human reviewing it, adding to it, or standing behind it, eventually becomes a liability.

When Google started using the acronym “E-A-T” in 2014 (now called “E-E-A-T”), it finally gave us a framework that shows how to even do SEO work without getting caught up in the loopholes. Since then, E-E-A-T has been misunderstood, misused, and treated as a checklist or a single ranking factor that works the same way for every site (it doesn’t). In 2021, I even wrote an article aimed specifically at debunking many of these misconceptions.

All of that being said, I still to this day believe E-E-A-T is the best framework we have for approaching our SEO/GEO strategies in ways that won’t be penalized or devalued later, and it gives us plenty of meaningful work to do once we focus on the right things. There’s a reason E-E-A-T is mentioned 120 times in the current version of Google’s Search Quality Rater Guidelines, and why Bing uses similar language, focusing on “quality and credibility,” in its own guidelines.

This type of work is people-first, meaning actual humans with lived knowledge sit at the center of the approach. It’s much harder than loophole-focused SEO, because it needs buy-in, time, and resources from the experts at the company, not just the SEO team operating behind the scenes. But the return is high, and it affects more channels than just organic. It tends to stand the test of time; it’s good for your users and your conversions; it appears to help with AI systems; and it’s unlikely to get you penalized (unless you apply a shortcut mindset to it, which isn’t really an E-E-A-T strategy at all). It’s also the opposite of what folks publicly say they hate about the impact SEO has had on Google’s results, from The Verge asking whether SEO experts ruined the internet to a 2024 study finding product review results increasingly full of SEO spam.

I’ve been preaching these same ideas for years, and I probably sound like a broken record to anyone who has followed me for a while (my MozCon 2022 talk was all about how to focus on real expertise, with numerous examples of real experts representing the brands they worked for). I even named my holistic approach to SEO/GEO the E-E-A-T Method and made it the core philosophy of my new consultancy, Algorythmic, because that’s how deeply I believe in the efficacy of this approach.

But this wasn’t always a big focus in how I approached SEO; it’s something I learned the hard way.

That 2018 Medic client I referred to before had been scaling a fast-growing library of health articles with no visible credentials from experts, and no sign of a real human behind any of it. When the update hit, Google’s Danny Sullivan pointed site owners back to the Search Quality Rater Guidelines (his tweet has since been deleted, but Marie Haynes wrote about his guidance at the time). So I spent months reading and re-reading Google’s guidelines. Being the nerd that I am, I even printed and laminated a copy and kept it on my desk (which I admitted on stage in 2019 at BrightonSEO). When I read it, the answer to our client’s challenge became obvious, and it was repeated throughout the guidelines: the site was heavily YMYL (Your Money or Your Life) and showed nowhere near enough E-A-T for the health topics it covered and the medical advice it provided.

The client wasn’t convinced at first, as this required a dramatic overhaul of their approach – so much so that we decided to part ways while they tried to bring back the site’s performance using their own methods. But after almost two years without recovering, the client came back to work with our team again. We worked together on a renewed SEO strategy, and about six months later, we relaunched the entire site, rebuilt from top to bottom around E-A-T, with human experts at the center: real doctors, real medical reviewers, and their original insights. The site climbed back to its previous levels after the re-platforming was complete. From the day the update hit, the full recovery process took more than three years. (This long recovery timeline is why I always warn sites to avoid getting hit in the first place!)

Back in January 2019, the night before my first-ever conference talk at SMX West (which was – surprise! – focused on E-A-T), I sat at the hotel bar studying Mark Traphagen’s work on author authority. He, along with Jennifer Slegg, had been documenting the history of “authorship” and “author authority” on Google over time. (Funny side note: I ended up meeting Mark in person for the first time at the conference breakfast the next morning, a few hours before I went on stage, which felt auspicious.) After my presentation, when an attendee asked what a small site should do if its writers aren’t well known, my answer was to “cultivate your authors’ profiles, even if it means starting from scratch,” which ruffled some feathers in a room filled with technical SEOs who didn’t all buy into the idea that Google could figure these things out. Yet nearly eight years of research and client results later, I’m even more convinced that it can.

A few months later, Google’s official guidance on core updates linked to my BrightonSEO deck on E-A-T as a recommended resource, along with work from a few other SEOs. This solidified for me that E-A-T was becoming a big priority for them. In 2020, I had the great privilege of digging into the patents that might explain how E-A-T works with the late, great Bill Slawski, whose knowledge of Google’s patents was unmatched. This exercise helped me understand a more technical explanation for how Google’s systems might recognize individual experts. The following year, I took the topic to the MozCon stage with a talk on how the E-A-T ecosystem has transformed organic search.

“Humanize your brand” and “keep a human in the loop” have become marketing clichés of their own, so I want to be specific. By “real humans,” I mean practitioners with genuine expertise or experience: the doctor who has treated the condition, the engineer who built the system, the plumber who owns a local plumbing business, or the patient who lived through the illness. They earn their audience naturally, and across platforms, by sharing insights that are honest, original, often opinionated, and based on real experience. You can usually tell them apart from someone who showed up to sell you something, and if a sale happens at all, it tends to follow from the trust they’ve built.

My approach, for SEO, AI search, and broader marketing, is to put these real people at the center of the strategy whenever possible. It’s also what I’ve employed with my own personal brand (more on that later).

I think this is the strategy most likely to survive whatever comes next, for a simple reason. Nearly every popular shortcut in the vicious cycle of SEO could be scaled. A real expert’s reputation can’t. It takes years of showing up, being right (and sometimes wrong, and open to admitting that) in public, and having other people vouch for you without needing to rely on inauthentic mentions or listicles calling yourself the best expert. As AI makes everything else cheaper to produce, I’d expect the value of that kind of earned reputation to keep climbing.

In April 2024, on the Authority Hacker podcast, I summed it up with one of the sentences I’ve said most often in my career:

“I’ve been talking about this for years: People like following people.”

Sidenote: Don’t mind the ghost opening the door behind me. That was my dog Marcy, who can never decide where she wants to lie down when I’m doing podcasts.

It’s no secret that folks on social platforms engage with other people far more than with brands. On LinkedIn, personal profiles outperform company pages by roughly 2x to 8x on impressions, depending on whose data you believe.

Here’s what real people bring to the table that AI can’t:

Across platforms, signs of a real human may be the clearest way to separate spam and automated content from the content that provides the most value.

A real human expert leaves evidence everywhere, and that footprint is easily detectable: photos from the conference they spoke at, video of the talk, a personal website (even a slightly neglected one), podcast interviews, years of social posts and replies, or journalists quoting them by name. I believe Google has systems in place to at least identify these signals, and likely reward them, from Knowledge Panels to the new Search profiles. The leaked Google documentation from May 2024 points in the same direction: it showed that Google stores the author of a document, and has an attribute called isAuthor that marks whether an entity mentioned on a page is also the author of that page.

The typical fake author, on the other hand, has a stock-looking AI-generated headshot, a two-sentence bio (if any), and no other evidence of their real existence anywhere on the web. This approach isn’t limited to small sites, either: in 2023, Sports Illustrated was found publishing product reviews under authors who didn’t appear to exist, including one whose headshot was for sale on a site that sells AI-generated portraits. In that same year, fake authors were one of the most common patterns I found among sites hit by the Helpful Content Update, and in October 2026, Google added this exact tactic to its helpful content documentation: “Fabricating creator profiles (such as by using AI-generated headshots, made-up names, or false credentials to make content appear as if it was written by human experts) is a form of deception.”

I predict that this trail of being a “real human” will matter even more as the web fills up with homogeneous vibe-coded sites. Anyone can now spin up a polished website in an afternoon, complete with a logo, a hundred blog posts, and a team page full of friendly AI-generated headshots. If you’ve looked at many of these sites, you’ve probably noticed they all start to look the same: the same purple gradient, the same three feature cards with emoji icons, the same “Trusted by” logo strip.

When a convincing-looking brand costs next to nothing and takes little time to build, polish alone doesn’t tell anyone very much anymore. What’s left are the signals that still take years to build: a real person or real people with real histories, who other real people have chosen to follow, quote, and recommend.

Since the 2018 Medic update, Google appears to have spent the past 8 years building systems that reward exactly that kind of trail. In 2019, I analyzed 64 sites that had clearly won or lost across the 2018 and 2019 core updates, checking each one for 30 on-page E-A-T signals and researching the credentials of the people writing their content. The winning sites were 258% more likely than the losing sites to use real experts on their content (with the usual caveat that this was a small sample, and correlation isn’t causation). Since then, Google has put many of those same observations into writing:

Real experts and real lived experiences appear to drive a big share of AI search citations, and you can see it in which sites get cited most. YouTube and Reddit are consistently the two most cited websites in Google’s AI Overviews, at 24.5% and 18.1% of citations among the top 50 cited domains in Ahrefs’ November 2026 analysis.

Other studies point to LinkedIn, too. In a Semrush study of 325,000 prompts earlier this year, LinkedIn was the second most cited domain in ChatGPT Search, Google AI Mode, and Perplexity, and 59% of the LinkedIn content cited in ChatGPT Search and AI Mode came from individual members rather than company pages.

This doesn’t surprise me – I’ve seen my LinkedIn posts and Pulse articles show up in Google’s AI search results immediately after publishing, like this test I did with a LinkedIn Pulse article about Google Discover. It earned the top ranking in AI Overviews and an AI Mode citation within seven hours of publishing.

In other words, a lot of the information AI search systems draw on to build responses comes from the places where real humans go to share what they actually know, like a creator on YouTube walking through how they fixed something or which product they like best, a Reddit thread full of firsthand experience, or a practitioner’s thoughtful LinkedIn post or Pulse article. Unfortunately, these same platforms are also being flooded with AI slop, and it’s not a secret.

YouTube and Reddit have been fairly explicit about what they want, and it also points to authentic human experiences. In July 2025, YouTube renamed its “repetitious content” monetization rule to “inauthentic content,” covering AI-generated videos made from generic templates “without adding the creator’s original, authentic insights or perspective,” and CEO Neal Mohan’s 2026 letter called out “AI slop” by name. Reddit CEO Steve Huffman wrote in February that “if you can’t easily distinguish a real person’s thoughts or recommendations from a bot, that trust erodes,” and a month later Reddit started labeling automated accounts. On both platforms, the most reliable path to visibility appears to be the one this whole post is about: be a real, identifiable person – sharing authentic and honest experiences – whom other people choose to trust.

I’ve seen firsthand what sharing publicly can do for a business. When I joined Amsive, I had never given an SEO talk on a stage or done anything public-facing in the industry. Since then, in almost nine years on the agency’s SEO team, I’ve published research on its blog under my own name, alongside podcast interviews, conference talks, webinars, and other marketing efforts on the agency’s behalf. That work has brought the agency links, traffic, and name recognition that keep growing long after each piece goes live. When I recently looked at the agency’s backlinks in Ahrefs, a few things stood out:

I’m sharing this because of where those links point: every one of them goes to the company. One person (or a team of people) sharing what they know under their own names can grow a company’s authority in a way that brand content on its own rarely does. I’ve seen the same pattern at countless other brands that put trusted experts at the front of their marketing, and I try to employ this same approach in my client strategies.

Of course, I’m not the only example of this, and others in the industry are seeing success with the same approach. For years, Wix had what the Ahrefs blog called “a bit of a bad reputation for SEO.” Plenty of SEOs would have steered clients away from it. Then Wix did something smart: it hired respected SEOs like Crystal Carter and Mordy Oberstein to represent the brand within the SEO community.

Crystal joined in 2022, and since then she has spoken at many major search and marketing conferences, co-hosted Wix’s SERP’s Up podcast, and published her own research on the Wix site. Today, when SEO publications write about whether Wix is good for SEO, they often point to her by name. That same Ahrefs article credits her and Mordy with pushing for “more SEO features and better communication.” About 1 in 20 sites linking to Wix’s SEO Hub mention Crystal by name, the podcast shows up in “best SEO podcasts” roundups from Backlinko and Ahrefs, and her expert page is the most-linked expert profile on the hub.

For a more famous example outside our industry, look at travel expert Rick Steves. He self-published his first travel guide in 1980, and he has spent about four months a year in Europe for decades, walking the routes himself and updating his guidebooks every year. That one person’s lived experience grew into a company with more than 100 employees, a PBS series that has run since 2000, a thriving forum and online community, a public radio show, and a tour program that takes more than 30,000 travelers to Europe each year.

I wrote about his site on LinkedIn this summer, calling it the ultimate embodiment of E-E-A-T and the perfect example of an expert-led marketing approach. He tells you – from firsthand experience – what’s overrated, overpriced, or skippable, and because he makes money from books and tours, his content is free from affiliate influence. His honesty is the product. Google’s AI Overviews often cite his website, and his YouTube and TikTok pages too.

Brands that can should start by identifying the real experts inside the company and investing in making them visible. In practice:

Two fair counterpoints, since this approach isn’t possible for every company: Some industries have compliance teams that make personal posting genuinely hard. And people may leave the company and take their personal brands with them. My answer is to try to build several voices instead of relying on one (my friend and colleague Viola Eva recently wrote about how they do exactly this at her company, Flow Agency). Furthermore, remember that any links, mentions, and coverage earned while someone represented the company can remain as valuable assets for the company, even after they move on.

In July 2023, I posted on LinkedIn that even if Google couldn’t tell AI content from human content, someone else could: “guess who else doesn’t like reading AI content? USERS.” The consumer research has since caught up. A Gartner survey this summer found that a majority of U.S. consumers say AI content has made them less trusting of brand messaging, and Emplifi’s 2026 research found that only 35% of Americans trust AI-generated content at all (not that everyone can necessarily tell the difference). I’d call it slop fatigue, and I think the platforms are finally responding to it (or at least trying to).

Every tactic that has blown up in this industry, from the links I bought in 2011 to the listicles and paid mentions all over the internet in 2026, was scaled for the sole purpose of driving visibility in search. That’s also, almost exactly, the list of things consumers say they dislike most about SEO. Real experts and experienced contributors have the opposite effect: they contribute the things that make the internet human, and the most popular, widely cited platforms are working hard to preserve their humanness in an internet flooded with AI slop.

There’s another reason this holds up: your reputation is ultimately decided by what other people say about you, not by what you say about yourself. One of the rater guideline passages I put on a slide back in 2019 reads: “When there is disagreement between what the website says about itself and what reputable independent sources say about the website, we’ll trust the independent sources.”

AI search is carrying that torch forward, as LLMs are getting better and better at determining someone’s reputation based on what others say about the brand or the person. That appears to increasingly include spotting self-promotion. Gemini now shows its reasoning steps, and in this example (h/t Gagan Ghotra), it directly evaluated whether “Best AI SEO agency” lists were self-promotional, with agencies ranking themselves highly, to judge how objective those rankings were. Being genuinely recommended by other people is the most sustainable way forward.

People like following people. That was true before Google, and it’ll still be true after whatever comes next. The brands that figure that out won’t need the next loophole.

This post was originally published on Lily Ray NYC Substack.

#7521. Reddit publishes guide to Super Bowl engagement trends

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Brands looking to engage with subreddit communities should begin well ahead of the 2027 game in order to map out effective approaches, per the platform.

Reddit published a new report which examines key NFL Super Bowl engagement stats and opportunities, and provides tips on how brands can tap into Super Bowl hype to maximize ad approaches.

The 12-page guide includes notes on Super Bowl and NFL engagement on Reddit, with overviews of how fans engage with the game across a range of related subreddit communities.

The guide also provides notes on how brands can build their Reddit presence, and get a handle on key trends in order to better target their approaches.

Reddit’s advice for brands essentially centers on choosing a specific content approach for their Super Bowl campaign, then honing in on the related questions will drive the most engagement.

Reddit said that brands should consider what feelings they want to evoke with their Super Bowl campaigns, and what rituals or language they want to use in order to relate to niche communities. Within this, brands should also consider how they can tell an authentic, meaningful story.

These elements link back to how Redditors engage, and by mapping out a strategic approach early that aligns with this, Reddit said that brands will be able to construct a more effective approach ahead of the Super Bowl hype in 2027.

Reddit’s guide includes a range of more specific notes on how to do this, and it could be a valuable planning tool for brands that plan to use the platform for their marketing efforts.
